# Good vs. bad — a worked skeleton and named anti-patterns

Read this alongside `document-quality.md`, `wireframe.md`, and `canvas.md`. It is
the bar an authored plan must clear.

## A good plan skeleton (UI work)

A plan for adding a bulk-archive action to a contacts list reads, top to bottom:

1. **Objective + done-criteria** — one short paragraph: what ships, what "done"
   means. For this broad-ish change, one concrete `<Screen surface="browser">`
   snapshot of the current list right under it, so a reviewer sees the starting
   point before any mechanics.
2. **Scope / non-goals** — prose. What is in the first cut, what is deferred.
3. **The change, as a comparable pair** — a `<Columns>` block with
   `<Column label="Before">` and `<Column label="After">`, each holding a
   `<Screen>` of the list header: the After adds a selection checkbox column and
   an `Archive selected` action in the existing toolbar's top-right slot; every
   other control is preserved so the delta is obvious. No `Before`/`After` pill
   baked into either frame — the column headers name the states.
4. **The file map** — an `<AnnotatedCode>` of the one load-bearing file (the list
   component), with two or three margin notes on the lines that change; a
   `<FileTree>` naming the handful of touched files with change badges.
5. **The decision** — a `<Callout tone="decision">` stating the chosen approach
   (optimistic archive with undo), with a `<Columns>` weighing it against the
   alternative you rejected.
6. **Verification** — prose naming the end-to-end smoke: select two rows, archive,
   confirm they leave the list and the undo toast restores them.
7. **One `<QuestionForm>`** at the very bottom for the single genuinely-open
   decision, with a `recommended` default.

Nothing repeats: the `<Screen>` pair shows the UI, the prose and code carry the
depth the pictures can't.

## A good plan skeleton (backend / architecture work)

No visual surface. The document opens with the objective and a one-paragraph
recommendation, then repeats a section rhythm per change: a short title, a
`<DataModel>` or `<Endpoint>` next to the prose that needs it, an
`<AnnotatedCode>` of the load-bearing file, an inline `<Mermaid>` or `<Diagram>`
only where a real two-dimensional relationship (layering, data flow) clarifies
something, and terse Problem/Solution/Why prose in the codebase's vocabulary. It
closes with a verification step and a bottom `<QuestionForm>` only if the next
direction is genuinely open.

## A good decision-review skeleton (recap genre)

A verdict batch — e.g. a taxonomy sign-off over N items, an audit, a PR-style
review — is a `mdx-visual-recap` artefact, not a plan. It reads, top to bottom:

1. **The review protocol** — a top `<Callout tone="decision">` stating what is
   being decided, how to record a verdict, and the **silence = accept the
   recommendation** convention. This is the first viewport: the reviewer learns
   what sign-off means before scrolling.
2. **A compact all-items `<Table>`** — one row per item (id, subject, verdict
   class, recommendation) so the whole batch is scannable at a glance before the
   detail.
3. **One `<Card>` per item**, tone = verdict class (colour is triage, meaning
   rides the badge/heading), a `badge` naming the class and `meta` chips for
   pack / confidence / recommended action. Inside each card, in order:
   - one or two sentences of verdict prose — why this recommendation;
   - the decisive evidence: a `<FieldDiff>` for the record change (null / absent
     / kept fields carry meaning), never a line `<Diff>` of a JSON string;
   - a `<Details>` drill-down holding the bulk evidence (full production entry,
     counterpart pack) — embedded, never linked out;
   - a `<ReviewChoice itemId>` capturing the per-item Accept / Reject / Discuss.
4. **A bottom `<QuestionForm>`** for only the genuinely balanced calls (rollout
   strategy, a schema question) — not a second copy of the per-item decisions.

The worked fixture for this skeleton lives at
`plans/mdx-review-blocks/plan.mdx` in the repo — read it as the concrete
example of every review block in situ.

## A good recap skeleton (recap genre)

A recap of a finished change (a branch, a thread's work) reads:

1. **A UI-impact headline** — wireframes (`<Screen>` / `<Columns>` before/after),
   but only when the diff changed rendered UI; skip it for pure backend work.
2. **A 1–3 paragraph outcome narrative** — what changed and why, in the
   codebase's vocabulary.
3. **Contract changes** — `<DataModel>` / `<Endpoint>` for any schema or API
   delta.
4. **A `<FileTree>` with change flags** — the change map.
5. **`## Key changes`** as one horizontal `<TabsBlock>` of `<Diff>` /
   `<AnnotatedCode>`, **3–8 tabs, ~150 lines per excerpt**, each with a one-line
   summary and a few line annotations. Optionally a `<ReviewChoice>` per tab
   when the recap doubles as a review gate.

## Named anti-patterns (never produce these)

- **Hard-coded hex instead of tokens.** A wireframe `html` with
  `style="background:#fff;color:#111"` (or a `font-family`) — breaks in dark mode.
  Use `var(--wf-paper)` / `var(--wf-ink)` and never set a font.
- **Forced desktop + mobile.** Emitting a `desktop` frame _and_ a `mobile` frame

caption>`) is the only place the state name belongs.

  frames).

  file-contract arrows, or architecture notes drawn inside the screen. Keep the
  screen pure; put those in a `<DesignBoard>` `<Annotation>`, a `<Diagram>`, or the
  prose.
- **A questions/decisions wall mid-document.** A second open-questions list, or a
  parallel "decisions" section above the bottom `<QuestionForm>`. There is exactly
  one questions block, at the very bottom.
- **A jargon-gated question.** A bottom `<QuestionForm>` leaning on labels the
  document coined, so a reviewer who skimmed the body cannot answer it: "Yes,
  fold it into slice 1". Gloss the dependency in `subtitle` and name the choice
  in the label: "Yes — build the meter in the same pass as the settings page". A
  `refs` chip does not rescue it: refs let a reviewer read the section a question
  turns on, they never carry meaning the question's own text leaves out.
- **A plan written as a changelog.** "Unlike the previous version…", "as discussed

I think I have enough grounding now—I'll skip the deep fixture check since I already know the vocabulary, though I note the lint tool exists at that script path. Now I want to move into the real judgment work: comparing what destination upstream V2's design is actually aiming for.

Upstream V2 is building a provider-fidelity execution model scoped to a single conversation with turn-scoped delegation, one-run tasks, pulled results, and lineage edges—deliberately not a workflow engine with gates, goals, dependencies, or holds. Loom, in contrast, is aiming for durable, inspectable organization of threads where work only starts when it should, can't silently stall, gets reviewed in the graph, and human holds actually hold.

Where they overlap: both treat delegated children as real, message-able threads with transcripts, both support waking without interrupting, both recover on restart, both are event-sourced with receipts and deterministic ids backed by a durable outbox, both have settle/snooze semantics, and both are converging on a shared cross-provider tool bridge. Where they diverge: V2 has no plan axis, no lanes, no dependencies, no gates, no goals, and no holds.

These absences aren't just missing features — some of V2's primitives actively contradict Loom's model: delegation needs a live parent turn while Loom's dispatcher creates and starts children between turns, V2 treats a task as a single run while Loom's gate loops re-engage the same reviewer thread repeatedly, V2 pulls results while Loom pushes a digest plus report path, and V2 shares a worktree across children while Loom isolates them. For the thread graph and delegation area specifically, I'm landing on a hybrid approach: adopt V2's AppThread, lineage, and ContextTransfer as the parentage record along with message.dispatch as the start primitive, but layer Loom's graph semantics—blockedBy, lanes, staged release, cascade, isolation, fan-in—on top as an extension rather than building on V2's turn-scoped, one-run delegate_task/Subagent records.

Loom children should be modeled as V2 app threads with subagent-relationship lineage created by the control plane, which conveniently aligns with how the sidebar already filters out subagent threads — matching Loom's own hiding of workstream children. I'm also weighing cost: redesigning around the engine coupling means touching the eight decider hunks on Orchestrator.ts, while porting the dispatcher, fan-in, and provisioner as self-contained modules re-seamed onto the existing event streaming and dispatch primitives.

V2's event replay off a sequence number removes the need for Loom's periodic-tick-plus-startup-pass workaround, though the full idempotent pass is still worth keeping since replay only simplifies rather than eliminates it. For worktree isolation, V2's deferred-start and worktree workspace strategy with prepared-run release and setup-script phases is essentially Loom's "provision at promotion" already expressed upstream for top-level threads — so I want to adopt that worktree mechanism for Loom children's provisioning while keeping Loom's branch naming, dirty-parent auto-commit, fan-in merge, and reaper logic. That's a port, not a redesign. Now turning to fan-in.

Upstream's merge_back is just context, not actual mechanism, so there's no real overlap there — it should be retained as-is. On forkFrom, upstream's native forkThread exists but runs as a throwaway process without identity replay, which conflicts with Loom's session naming, so that needs to be handled separately.

Then moving to the agent tool surface and transport layer, both systems converge on the same destination — a T3-owned extension bridging server tools into pi over the same MCP credential — so the verdict is to adopt upstream's transport (the MCP toolkit with dynamic discovery) while retaining Loom's tool catalogue and tool-definition-as-data authoring by registering Loom's tools as MCP toolkits on the shared endpoint.

Weighing this against upstream's bespoke REST approach, I'm seeing the tradeoff: going MCP-native is provider-neutral and gives preview/PR toolkits to pi for free with one unified credential and bridge, but it carries a real rename cost since every role, skill, and memory reference bare tool names, and Loom's hand-authored prompt guidance would need a new carrier via MCP's description field under pi's tool prefix — which cuts against the brief's "smallest end state" principle, so I'm considering the alternative of just running Loom's extension alongside upstream's as a second loaded extension instead.

Actually, I realize the prefix naming is controlled by upstream's own extension source file, so Loom could patch that to register bare names for its toolkit — a small hunk — though there's also a presentation layer file and the role profile's active-tools list that would need corresponding changes.

For `enable_toolset`, upstream's extension lacks a `setActiveTools` call, but Loom could add its own `session_start` hook that fetches the active-tools profile from the server using the thread's credential — making the server the single source of truth rather than relying on per-instance env vars. I'm also working out how to avoid overlap between `delegate_task` and `t3_thread_*` by withholding the orchestration capability from Loom-launched sessions and granting a separate workstream capability instead.

Since `McpSessionRegistry.issue` is what grants orchestration, Loom's hunk would simply issue workstream and skip orchestration for its threads, which cleanly hides the orchestrator toolkit and prevents `delegate_task` from ever being callable — avoiding a competing delegation model in the prompt. But this also hides other orchestration-gated tools like thread read/list/search and the pending-request queue, some of which could still be useful (e.g., reading threads for consulting alternatives), so I'm leaning toward hiding the whole surface for now and possibly re-exposing read-only thread tools later.

My verdict is a hybrid approach: adopt the MCP transport and bridge, keep Loom's catalogue and authoring layer, replace REST with an MCP toolkit, and withhold upstream's orchestration capability from Loom threads. The porting cost looks manageable since the handler layer only talks to the engine through dispatch calls and snapshot reads, so the real work is at the edge — converting routes into toolkit handlers and wiring the engine calls into Loom's snapshot extensions.

But I'm second-guessing whether MCP toolkit is really better than keeping REST, since the goal is the smallest possible end state — two separate bridges mean duplicated auth conventions and more total code, whereas consolidating into one bridge trims things down substantially, especially if some of Loom's custom tools like ask_user_question can map natively onto V2's user input request flow instead of needing their own long-polling mechanism.

So I'm leaning toward recommending adoption of the MCP transport and porting Loom's tools into an MCP toolkit — it's provider-neutral, unifies credentials, and eliminates both the REST routes and Loom's custom extension transport entirely.

On naming, I'd default to keeping bare tool names rather than prefixing them, since roles, skills, memories, and docs all reference them that way and a rename would ripple everywhere for no real gain. For lifecycle and state, V2's richer run/attempt/node runtime axis is more honest than Loom's derived executing/starting/idle/none projection, though V2 lacks a plan lane, attention, or liveness concepts — so I'd adopt V2's runtime model while treating Loom's projection as something layered on top.

I'd map Loom's session+turn onto V2's Run/activityRunStatus, but keep Loom's heartbeat mechanism (writing it off the V2 adapter event stream, since V2 has no heartbeat equivalent). Loom's plan lane and attention axes should stay as extension fields/events, and the dispatcher rails, liveness sweep, and exhaustion resume logic should become reactors sitting on top of V2's stream. There's a genuine semantic collision though: V2's message.dispatch only supports queue_after_active, while Loom's requireIdle needs a "defer and recompute later" semantics for coalesced digests — something V2 doesn't natively provide.

The simplest fix is a small Loom-only pre-dispatch check inside the per-thread lock, implemented as a Loom internal command variant (dispatchMode: start_if_idle) that the decider treats as a no-op-with-receipt when a run is already live — roughly a 20-line addition to the decider switch. For the stuck-launch CAS and turn-start-fail problem, I'm noting that V2 already addresses this with RunAttempt, preparing/starting states, an effect outbox with retries, and a specific fix commit confirming runs no longer get stuck.

Given that, several V1 workarounds look like candidates for removal once V2's outbox/attempt model is verified: stuck-launch recovery and turn-start-fail should be marked "verify then likely drop." Restart recovery can migrate to a Loom policy hook layered on V2's own ProviderRuntimeRecoveryService and restart continuation, preserving Loom's rules about not continuing flagged/cancelled/parked threads and re-delivering undelivered kickoffs. Settlement blockers become a small hunk in V2's thread.auto-settle decider case, since ThreadSettlementService is server-owned and Loom's two blockers can port over similarly.

I'm weighing the cost of redesigning engine attachment for the axes versus preserving exactly-once wake receipts — V2's command receipts should carry the same semantics as V1, though I need to check whether zero-event successes still persist a receipt, which may require a hunk if not. Idle-only turn start should carry over unchanged. For review gates, there's no upstream structure to inherit, but Loom's approach of treating the gate as a graph edge with the same reviewer thread across rounds and control-plane routing is distinct enough that the verdict is to retain Loom as-is on top of V2.

# Pull 9 strategy — adopt Orchestration V2, re-express Loom on top

Loom is a Pi-first fork of `pingdotgg/t3code` whose product is an orchestration layer: goals, a shared task tree, and a workstream graph of durable threads with roles, briefs, dependencies, review gates, attention flags, plan lanes, liveness detection, isolated worktrees with fan-in, reports, and consult/notify. Upstream has now shipped **Orchestration V2** (commit `de34391427`, 1,914 files) with a native Pi adapter, and deleted the V1 engine Loom's layer is welded to. This document decides, area by area, whether upstream is heading where Loom is heading — and therefore whether Loom adopts upstream's mechanism and re-expresses its guarantees on it, or keeps its own — then rolls that up into one mechanism for pull 9.

**Done** means Carl has recorded a verdict on each of the twelve areas below, chosen the overall mechanism, and answered the open questions, so a follow-on planner can write the implementation plan for the chosen phases.

<Callout tone="decision">
**How to review this.** Each area ends in a `ReviewChoice`; Accept means the verdict and cost class stand, Reject means the follow-on plan must take a different path for that area (say which in the note), Discuss parks it. Silence accepts the recommendation. The overall mechanism and the questions the evidence cannot settle are in the single form at the bottom. Card colour is triage only: **blue = adopt upstream**, **amber = hybrid**, **purple = retain Loom, re-expressed on V2**, **grey = retain Loom as-is because upstream has nothing there**.
</Callout>

## The recommendation in one paragraph

**Re-platform, staged.** Take `upstream/main` as the base including V2 and the Pi V2 adapter, and re-express Loom's layer as a V2 extension: Loom's thread fields, commands and events as a sidecar contract on V2's store; Loom's decider rules as a delegation arm plus about six marked hunks in upstream's decider; Loom's control-plane workers (dispatcher, fan-in, liveness, exhaustion resume) re-seamed onto V2's event stream and shell snapshot; Loom's agent tools moved from bespoke REST routes onto upstream's MCP bridge as a Loom toolkit, with upstream's `delegate_task` family **withheld** from Loom threads so there is one delegation model in every prompt. The evidence says upstream is heading to the same destination as Loom on the *substrate* — durable children as real threads, event-sourced commands with receipts, a durable outbox, restart reconciliation, a shared tool bridge, a separate fork migration ledger — and to a genuinely different (or absent) destination on the *workflow*: no plan axis, no dependencies, no gates, no goals, no human holds, no liveness, no per-child worktree. Adopting the substrate and retaining the workflow is therefore the right split. "Retain" is not a cheap alternative: V2 rewired the web, mobile and client-runtime around V2 contracts and gates `/ws` on protocol version 2, so keeping V1 means freezing the whole client and the store mobile app, i.e. a hard fork. The staging is a feature freeze on Loom's orchestration layer, production staying on pre-pull-9 Loom, a long-lived integration branch, and a cut-over gated by a real Pi workstream smoke test. Pull 8 (PR #323) should land first.

## What the evidence says, in five facts

The four research reports in `docs/upstream-sync/27-pull9-v2-alignment/` are facts-only; these are the five that carry the decision.

1. **V2 is an execution-fidelity model for one conversation, not a workflow engine.** Children share the parent's worktree; there are no dependencies, no staging, no cascade cancellation of app-owned children, no gates, no goals or tasks, no stall detection, no human holds; a role is a one-sentence prefix; the parent is woken with a generic "call `task_status`" pointer (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md`, §A, §D, §E, §I and the closing *Design centre of gravity*).
2. **Loom is physically separated from V1 files but semantically welded to V1's vocabulary.** 24 commands, 25 events, a `goal` aggregate, about 35 projection columns, 45 migrations, about 20 snapshot-query methods, 8 in-place decider edits and 3 engine-invariant changes (`02-loom-inventory.md`, §0 "One structural fact"). The control-plane workers are portable modules on narrow seams.
3. **The Pi driver decision is downstream of the V2 decision.** Upstream's Pi adapter implements `ProviderAdapterV2`; Loom's implements the deleted V1 shape. If V2 lands, Loom's driver must be rewritten against V2 anyway, and upstream's adapter *is* that rewrite, fixture-tested on pi 1.0.0 (`03-pi-driver-comparison.md`, Headline 1).
4. **The merge is a merge plus a port, whatever the strategy.** 336 conflicted paths: 155 textual (pull-7 shaped, fits the pull-7 tooling) and 181 structural (95 modify/delete, 86 directory-rename relocations) with nothing on the other side to merge into; about 57,000 Loom lines sit on the deleted engine; 92 contract names used by 241 files vanish; about 125 files end up with dangling imports; `config.ts` silently auto-merges to `statev2.sqlite` (`04-trial-merge-surface.md`).
5. **Pull 8 barely shrank the problem** (348 to 336 conflicts) because it only removed the pre-V2 drift. The V2 surface is unchanged in size and the 110 upstream commits since the earlier dry run barely added to it.

## Verdict table

<Table
  columns={["Area", "Same destination?", "Verdict", "Cost class", "Loom guarantee that must survive"]}
  rows={[
    ["A · Thread graph and delegation", "Partly — durable children, lineage, worktree-prepared launches; nothing for dependencies, lanes, cascade, fan-in", "Hybrid: V2 thread + lineage + prepared-run launch as the record and start primitive; Loom graph semantics as an extension", "Redesign (engine attachment) + port (workers)", "Start only when deps are done and lane released; dependents start from a tree containing merged output; cancel cascades"],
    ["B · Agent tool surface and transport", "Yes — a T3-owned pi extension bridging server tools over the per-thread MCP credential", "Adopt upstream's MCP bridge; retain Loom's catalogue and tool-def-as-data as a Loom MCP toolkit; withhold upstream's orchestration toolkit from Loom threads", "Port", "Caller identity from the credential, never a parameter; lean leaf surface with dormant families; server render is the source of truth"],
    ["C · Lifecycle and state model", "Partly — V2's run/attempt/node model is a better runtime axis; nothing for plan lane, attention, liveness", "Adopt V2's runtime axis; retain plan lane + attention + dispatcher rails + liveness as an extension; drop the V1-era launch workarounds V2 obsoletes", "Redesign (axes' engine hooks) + port (rails)", "No silent halt; agents write only plan + raised attention; exactly-once, idle-only wakes"],
    ["D · Review gates and verdict routing", "No — upstream has guidance only (re-delegate per round, fresh sessions)", "Retain Loom, re-expressed on V2 (routes, submit, rounds, reopen, yield)", "Port", "No outcome silently becomes done; a same-turn raise refuses a completing submit; the loop runs without waking the orchestrator"],
    ["E · Goals and task tree", "Upstream has nothing", "Retain Loom as-is; store goals in Loom's own tables rather than as a V2 aggregate", "Port (with a simplification)", "Every session has a goal; the tree is a glanceable shape; a child touches only its branch"],
    ["F · Context transfer", "Partly — explicit transfers, agent-to-thread send, native fork, thread read", "Hybrid: adopt message.dispatch with senderThreadId + notification, thread.fork and ContextTransfer; retain reports, workstream_list, consult_thread; drop Loom's defer queue and provenance columns", "Port", "Information moves cheapest first (report, graph, consult, then jsonl); a notify never interrupts"],

## Area A — Thread graph and delegation

**Same destination? Partly.** Upstream and Loom agree that a delegated child is a *real app thread* with a transcript a human can open and message (V2 `creationSource:"mcp"` children take messages; `02-loom-inventory.md` §A intent), that its parentage is recorded, and that launching into a prepared worktree is a server workflow (`message.dispatch` with `dispatchMode:{type:"defer_start", workspaceStrategy}` → `prepared-run.release`, with setup-script phases and retry — `01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §A "Held / staged creation"). They disagree on everything above that: V2 has no dependency or ordering between children, no held lane, no cascade cancellation of app-owned children, no per-child worktree for delegated tasks, and merge-back is context not code.

**Verdict — hybrid.** Adopt V2's `AppThread` + `lineage` (`parentThreadId`, `relationshipToParent:"subagent"`, `rootThreadId`) as the parentage record, and V2's `message.dispatch` (`start_immediately` / `defer_start` with a `worktree` workspace strategy) as the kickoff primitive. Retain Loom's graph semantics as an extension: `blockedBy`, plan lane, `spawnGeneration`, `graphKey`, `isolation`, `fanInState`, `routes`, `anchorTaskId`, `kickoffBriefPath`, `reportPath` as Loom fields on the thread; `thread.spawn` / `thread.scaffold` / `thread.dependencies.set` / `thread.plan-lane.set` / `thread.fanin.set` as Loom commands in the decider arm; the dispatcher's promotion rail and the fan-in reactor as Loom reactors on `streamDomainEvents`.

Two things follow that are easy to miss:

- **Loom children are not V2 "delegated tasks".** `delegated_task.request` requires a blocking parent run owned by the calling session (`parent_not_active`), publishes the first child run's output as the stable result, and never reopens. Those invariants contradict Loom's control-plane-created, dependency-gated, re-engageable children. So Loom never uses `delegate_task` or `OrchestrationV2Subagent` rows for workstream children; the Loom `thread.spawn` arm nests upstream's `thread.create` with lineage set (the command has no lineage fields today, so the arm sets them the way `dispatchDelegatedTaskRequest` does) and emits Loom events in the same transaction. V2 already uses this nesting pattern internally (`Orchestrator.ts:9884` "nested: dispatchDelegatedTaskRequest already writes child events").
- **V2's lineage gives Loom two things for free.** Sidebar filtering: upstream hides `relationshipToParent:"subagent"` threads (`filterSidebarV2VisibleThreads`), which is exactly Loom's "children are invisible in the sidebar" rule. And `streamStoredEventsFrom(afterSequence)` offers replay that V1's `streamDomainEvents` lacked — the dispatcher's periodic tick and startup pass were partly a workaround for that; the full idempotent pass stays (it is the right design) but the catch-up machinery shrinks.

**What survives, what is a V1 workaround.** Survives: both start gates (deps `done` ∧ lane released) and the atomic kickoff + `in_progress` write; cancel cascade (emits `run.interrupt` per live descendant inside the arm); subtree archive/delete cascade (hunks on V2's `thread.archive|unarchive|delete`); worktree isolation with branch naming `ws/<parentBranch>/<role>-<id8>`, dirty-parent snapshot commit, and fan-in by `git merge --no-ff` with conflict → wake parent; worktree GC; honest per-turn diffs (start-of-turn baseline — attaches to V2's `checkpoint.captured` rather than the deleted `CheckpointReactor`). Workaround made unnecessary: Loom's own worktree provisioning *call site* — the provision-at-promotion step becomes a `defer_start` with `workspaceStrategy:{type:"worktree", baseRef, branch}` so upstream's `ThreadLaunchService` does the worktree creation and setup script, and Loom's `WorktreeProvisioner` shrinks to branch naming and the snapshot commit. `forkFrom` (acknowledge-then-fork) is decided in Area L.

**Users gain** upstream's prepared-run progress UI and retry for worktree setup, lineage in upstream's panel and mobile sheets, and provider-neutral children (any V2 adapter). **Users lose** nothing in the model; the cost is that promotion, cascade and fan-in attach to V2 in new places.

**Cost class — redesign for the attachment, port for the workers.** The dispatcher (3,677 lines), fan-in (1,026), reaper (459) and shared libs (`workstreamDependencies.ts`, `workstreamGraph.ts`, `workstreamIsolation.ts`) move with logic intact; the attachment (spawn arm with nested create, kickoff-as-`message.dispatch`, cascade hunks) is new code of a few hundred lines replacing the equivalent V1 hunks.

## Area B — Agent tool surface and transport

**Same destination? Yes.** Both servers write a T3-owned pi extension at session open, pass it with `--extension`, and give it a per-session bearer from the same `McpSessionRegistry` credential; both forward `pi.registerTool` calls to the server over HTTP (`03-pi-driver-comparison.md` Headline 2, §2). Loom's `T3_WORKSTREAM_ENDPOINT` is literally upstream's MCP endpoint minus `/mcp`. The difference is contract: upstream is a real MCP client with dynamic `tools/list` discovery and `mcp__t3-code__*` names; Loom is a static list of 23 hand-authored tools POSTing to bespoke `/provider-tools/*` REST routes with server-rendered text.

**Verdict — adopt upstream's transport, retain Loom's catalogue; withhold upstream's orchestration toolkit from Loom threads.** Loom's tool definitions (`providerToolDefs.ts`, 1,003 lines of description, snippet, guidelines, schema, `errorMode`) become a `WorkstreamToolkit` (and `GoalToolkit`) registered on `/mcp` beside upstream's ten toolkits, gated by the `workstream` capability Loom's driver already requests. The handlers (`WorkstreamSpawnHttp.ts` 4,061, `GoalTaskHttp.ts` 428, `GoalHandoffHttp.ts` 333, `ThreadForkHttp.ts`, `UserInputHttp.ts`) already talk to the engine only through `engine.dispatch` (14 sites) and five snapshot reads, so the port is at the edge: route → toolkit handler, `engine.dispatch` → `OrchestratorV2.dispatch`, `getShellSnapshot` → V2's `getShellSnapshot` joined with Loom's sidecar. Upstream's MCP tool `description` carries Loom's prose; the bridge's generic one-line guideline is replaced by the def's `promptSnippet` via a small hunk in `piT3McpExtensionSource.ts`.

The genuine collision is **`delegate_task` / `t3_thread_*` beside `workstream_spawn` / `notify_thread`**: both surfaces land in one prompt unless one is filtered. Resolution: for Loom-launched sessions the credential is issued with `workstream` and **without** `orchestration`, so the `OrchestratorToolkit` and `ThreadToolkit` are not listed to the agent at all (they `requireCapability("orchestration")`). One hunk in `McpSessionRegistry.issue`, no filtering in the extension, and `delegate_task` — which would create a child sharing the parent's worktree, with no gate, no lane and no brief — cannot be called. The shared orchestration instructions that describe `delegate_task` are then also skipped (they are appended "only when the session has an MCP credential"; the hunk keys them on `orchestration` specifically). Whether to later re-expose upstream's *read-only* thread tools (`t3_thread_read`, `t3_thread_list`, `t3_thread_search`) is an open question below.

**What Loom's extension still owns.** Loom keeps its own small extension loaded as a second `--extension` beside upstream's (both load cleanly per report 03): the role tool profile via `pi.setActiveTools` at `session_start` (select-not-restrict, so dormant families stay one `enable_toolset` away), `enable_toolset` itself, the prompt-debug sidecar, and the search guard folded in. The profile no longer travels as per-thread env (`T3_ACTIVE_TOOLS` has no carrier in upstream's per-instance env); the extension fetches it with the credential at `session_start`, which is more honest about "the server render is the single source of truth". The two extensions have disjoint responsibilities — bridge and permission gate versus profile and guard — which is not a dual-shape coexistence.

**Users gain** provider-neutral tools (a future non-Pi V2 adapter gets the workstream tools by issuing the capability), upstream's preview and PR toolkits in pi for free, one credential story and one env convention, and the retirement of about 1,200 lines of REST routing and bespoke transport. **Users lose** the bare tool names unless a small naming hunk keeps them (open question; default keep bare names, because roles, skills, memories and habits all name `workstream_submit`, and the `mcp__t3-code__` prefix is prompt noise).

**Cost class — port.**

## Area C — Lifecycle and state model

**Same destination? Partly.** V2's `Run` / `RunAttempt` / `ExecutionNode` / `ProviderSession` states and the shell's `activityRunStatus` are a more honest **runtime axis** than Loom's derived `executing / starting / idle / none` projection over V1 session + latest turn, and V2's settle/snooze/wake model is the one Loom already adopted in the sidebar rehome. V2 has **no plan axis**, **no attention axis**, and **nothing** that detects a running turn making no progress (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §C "Stuck runs, idle and stall detection").

**Verdict — adopt the runtime axis; retain plan lane and attention as extension fields with their authority rules; retain the dispatcher rails and liveness; delete the V1 launch workarounds V2 obsoletes.**

- **Plan lane and attention** (`planned → ready → in_progress → yielded → done | cancelled`; stored `error | awaiting_acceptance | needs_guidance`; derived `awaiting_approval | awaiting_input | brief-needed`) are Loom fields and events in the decider arm with the single authority chokepoint intact: `in_progress`, `yielded` and `error` are control-plane-only (the `server:` command-id guard works unchanged on V2 command ids). Derived attention is recomputed at the read boundary from V2's `pendingRuntimeRequest` instead of V1 open-request rows — a simplification.
- **Turn-start rules** (§7 clear-all stored attention on any turn start; `ready`/`yielded` revert to `in_progress`; sticky terminal; started-dependents warning) become **one hunk cluster in V2's `message.dispatch` case** — the single place every run begins — replacing today's spread across `thread.turn.start`.
- **Human stop raises `needs_guidance`, orchestrator stop does not** → hunk in `run.interrupt` keyed on the command-id prefix, as today.
- **Idle-only wakes.** This is a collision. Loom's `requireIdle` *defers* a wake to a busy parent without a receipt so the dispatcher recomputes a fresh digest on the next idle; V2's `message.dispatch` offers `queue_after_active` (durably queues the stale text) or `steer_active`, never "drop and let the caller retry". Resolution: a Loom `dispatchMode:{type:"start_if_idle"}` handled in the `message.dispatch` hunk as a no-op-with-receipt when a run is live. About twenty lines; it is the one engine-invariant change the control plane cannot do without.
- **Exactly-once wake receipts.** V2 has `orchestration_v2_command_receipts` keyed by `commandId` — the same witness Loom's rails read. Verify that V2 persists a receipt for a zero-event success (Loom's "no-event success persists an accepted receipt" rule, `OrchestrationEngine.ts:344–389`); if not, that is the second engine-invariant hunk.
- **Settlement blockers** (`yielded`, any non-terminal descendant; finished root settles promptly; human send unsettles) → hunk in V2's `thread.auto-settle` case and `ThreadSettlementService`. Same shape as today.
- **Liveness sweep** (dead / waiting / stalled / spinning, 60 s cadence, one informed nudge then escalate) ports as-is; its heartbeat is written from the V2 adapter event stream (`provider-turn.updated`, `turn-item.updated`) into a Loom table instead of from V1 ingestion.

**Workarounds V2 makes unnecessary — verify, then delete:** stuck-launch CAS repair (`stuckLaunchRecovery.ts`, 427 lines + decider case) and `thread.turn-start.fail` (40) addressed a V1 session wedged `starting` with no turn; V2's `preparing | starting` run states, `RunAttempt` with `provider_recovery`, the durable effect outbox with `EffectWorker` claims, and upstream's `6108ef3d3d` "runs no longer get stuck" hardening target the same failure. Loom's pending-steer stash (`pendingSteering.ts`) covered pi's in-process steer queue across restarts; V2 moved queued and steered messages server-side. Loom's exhaustion resume stays (V2's `limitRecovery` covers provider usage limits, not Loom's per-account failover targets), re-anchored on V2's run error.

**Users gain** V2's run/attempt detail in the timeline and the settle/wake polish. **Users lose** nothing; the no-silent-halt invariant is preserved with less machinery.

**Cost class — redesign for the axes' hooks (new attachment points, same rules), port for the rails and sweep.**

## Area D — Review gates and verdict routing

**Same destination? No.** Upstream has nothing structural — no gate, verdict, round, cap or reviewer binding. Its guidance is the opposite design: re-call `delegate_task` per round with the prior findings, a fresh reviewer session each time, and never continue a review on `childThreadId` (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §D). Loom's design is a first-class, outcome-conditional loop edge in the graph that runs coder → reviewer → coder to resolution **without waking the orchestrator**, round-capped, with yield-to-orchestrator as the default for anything unexpected (`docs/design/workstream-review-gates.md`).

**Verdict — retain Loom, re-expressed on V2.** `routes`, `gateRounds`, `pendingRework`, `lastOutcome`, `reportPath` are Loom fields; `thread.work.submit` and gate traversal are Loom commands in the arm; `routeWorkSubmit` (`packages/shared/src/workstreamGraph.ts`, 576 lines, pure) is untouched. The one V1 hunk this area needed — `reopen` on `thread.turn.start` reverting a `done` coder to `in_progress` atomically — disappears as a hunk: the gate-traverse arm emits the Loom lane event and nests the `message.dispatch` in one transaction, the same way the spawn arm nests `thread.create`. Per-round report files, deterministic `server:workstream-gate:<R>:<round>:<leg>` ids, the raise-then-complete refusal (10 of 20 audited raises had been erased by their own submit), the bypass guard on a self-issued `set_lane done`, and the suppressions (`isWaitingInGate`, `isMemberOfUnresolvedGate`) all port with the dispatcher.

**Users gain** nothing from upstream here; the review-round guidance in upstream's shared instructions is not injected into Loom threads (Area B). **Users lose** nothing.

**Cost class — port.**

## Area E — Goals and task tree

**Same destination? Upstream has nothing.** No durable objective above a thread, no shared tree, no agent tool to read or edit one. Upstream's adjacent things — per-run todo lists, proposed plans, scheduled tasks, the parent's `Subagent` rows — are not goals (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §E).

**Verdict — retain Loom as-is, with one simplification: goals and tasks as plain Loom tables, not a V2 aggregate.** Under V1 the goal was an aggregate kind in the shared event store with its own stream because the V1 read model folded the whole log from sequence 0 on boot and the goal needed to survive that. V2's projections are SQL tables maintained by a projector, and V2's event table is keyed by `thread_id`; a goal has no thread. Giving the goal a place in V2's log means either a Loom-added column on upstream's events table or a parallel Loom event table — both are ceremony for a record whose history nobody replays. The smaller correct end state is `loom_goals` and `loom_goal_tasks` written directly by the goal tool handlers (with `clientRequestId` idempotency at the toolkit edge, which upstream's MCP layer already provides via `stableCommandId`), and the shell-stream `goal-upserted` / `goal-removed` items broadcast from the handler. The task-tree libs (`goalTaskTree.ts`, `goalTaskMarkdown.ts` round-trip identity, `goalTaskRender.ts`, the 300-character register cap, anchors with branch scoping, the echo-after-every-mutation) are unchanged. This is recorded as an open question because it is a real design choice the evidence does not settle.

The hooks Loom needs from the engine are the same four as today and land as hunks in V2's decider: `project.delete` refuses or cascades active goals; archiving a goal's last active thread archives the goal (and unarchive reverses); renaming the sole thread renames the goal; attaching a goal to a thread attaches it to goal-less descendants. The emergent goal (side-channel generation on turn 1 or 2) rides V2's effect outbox as a Loom effect kind beside `thread-title.generate`. Prompt injection is Area G. `goal_handoff` and `goal_continue` create staged roots and siblings through the Loom spawn arm.

**Users gain** nothing from upstream; **users lose** the goal's event history (which no surface reads).

**Cost class — port, smaller afterwards.**

## Area G — Prompt composition

**Same destination? Partly.** Upstream injects shared text into pi through the extension's `before_agent_start` and gives pi no per-thread prompt (`acceptsSystemContext:false`; `03-pi-driver-comparison.md` §3). Loom composes, per thread, the work-model addendum, thread-identity clause, role overlay, shipping policy, role catalogue, goal context and relocation clause, and passes it as `--append-system-prompt` argv so the launch bytes are captured as identity and a `forkFrom` child replays them for a byte-identical cache prefix.

**Verdict — retain what Loom composes; re-express how it is delivered.** The composition moves from the deleted `ProviderCommandReactor.startProviderSession` to a Loom hook where V2 opens sessions (`ProviderSessionManager`), producing the same text. Delivery: a Loom field on `ProviderAdapterV2OpenSessionInput` (`appendSystemPrompt`, `skills`, `extensions`) that `buildPiRpcLaunch` turns into `--append-system-prompt`, `--skill` and the second `--extension`. **Same destination? ## Area L — Provider registry and the Pi driver

**Same destination? Yes for the registry and the adapter contract; no for economics and operations.** Upstream's `ProviderDriver` SPI now requires an `orchestrationAdapter: ProviderAdapterV2Shape`, and `PiAdapterV2` + `PiRpc` (about 3,500 lines, 67 tests, 8 recorded live-pi transcripts through a replay harness) is the V2 Pi adapter already written. Loom's `PiDriver.ts` (2,959 lines, 152 tests including six that run the real patched pi) implements the deleted V1 shape and cannot plug into V2 (`03-pi-driver-comparison.md`, Headline 1 and the base-choice assessment).

**Verdict — adopt upstream's adapter; retain Loom's economics and operations as hunks and sidecar modules; resolve session identity in upstream's favour with a deterministic first file name.**

Adopted with the adapter: `agent_settled` + idle-probe turn settlement, extension dialogs → approvals and questions, native non-destructive rollback via `fork(entryId)`, native fork and fork-from-turn, `readThreadSnapshot` for handoffs, per-model thinking, live usage, the retry and compaction rows, the unsolicited-activity guard, `set_session_name`, `$skill` expansion.

Retained as Loom hunks or modules (sizes from report 03's list): bundled patched pi resolution and manual-only maintenance (`pi update --self` disabled); `--session-id <threadId>` at first launch; Loom open-session fields → argv (Area G); quota failover, tier-2 effective-model resolution, `model.rerouted`, the T3 slow-retry tier and `quota_exhausted` for the resume sweep — **re-anchored on `agent_settled`, not ported** (about 600 interleaved lines, the largest single item); cost and model attribution on usage (`costUsd` has no slot in V2 `tokenUsage` — a contract hunk); the codex → Anthropic tool-id sanitiser; account quota pollers; `PI_CACHE_RETENTION`; `queue_update` display. Stdout backpressure and `rawInput` merging are kept only if a measurement under V2 shows they are still needed.

**Session identity — the deepest collision.** Upstream's identity is the session file *path* (`nativeThreadRef`), resumed by RPC `switch_session`, rolled back by `fork(entryId)` which creates a new file; Loom's is a deterministic `*_<threadId>.jsonl`, resumed by patched `--session <file> --cwd`, rolled back by in-place truncation, and about ten Loom modules locate sessions by that name. Two identity schemes is dual-shape; the resolution is: the first launch passes `--session-id <threadId>` so the file is still recognisable by name and `$PI_SESSION_FILE` (pi-native) still works for the identity clause, but **`nativeThreadRef` on the V2 provider thread is the authority**, and the ten consumers (`workstreamAsk`, `threadResolve`, `stallContext`, `workstreamLaunchIdentity`, the dispatcher, the fork and handoff handlers, the drafters) resolve the file through it. Rollback follows upstream (new file, ref updated). Patch 0001 is **extended to RPC `switch_session`** (pi's `switchSession` already accepts `cwdOverride`; the RPC handler just never passes it) so resume after a reaped worktree keeps working through upstream's resume path; the `PiCwdOverride` contract test is ported to that path.

**`forkFrom` (acknowledge-then-fork).** Upstream's `forkThread` forks natively in a throwaway process but does not replay launch identity, so the cache-prefix guarantee needs Loom's identity sidecar on top: retain `workstreamLaunchIdentity.ts` and replay argv in the Loom launch hunk when `forkFromThreadId` is set.

**Pi version.** Upstream recommends pi 1.0 and recorded fixtures on 1.0.0; Loom pins 0.99.2 with two patches. Both patches are still needed against 1.0.2 (`--cwd` absent, `auth.json` still written non-atomically). Default: bump to 1.0.2 and regenerate the patch bundle, because the adapter was written and tested against 1.0 behaviour.

**`PiSettings` collisions**: `enabled` default `false` upstream vs `true` in Loom (keep Loom's — Pi-first); `binaryPath:"pi"` resolves the global binary upstream vs the bundled patched copy in Loom (keep Loom's); `customModels` as objects upstream vs strings in Loom (adopt upstream's shape, migrate); the pi-only registry (one hunk, unchanged).

**Users gain** robustness (settlement, rollback, dialogs, fixtures) and the end of a 2,959-line driver Loom maintained alone. **Users lose** in-place rollback (fine — upstream's is non-destructive) and must accept a pi bump.

**Cost class — redesign-sized port.** The adapter is free; the re-anchoring of failover/retry and the identity re-pointing are the risk, and the latter fails *silently* (amnesia) when wrong, so it gets its own contract test.

## Overall mechanism options

The measured surface is the same under every option: 155 textual conflicts that fit the pull-7 method, and a port of the orchestration, provider-adapter, projection-persistence and V1-contract areas because no `ours` or `theirs` side compiles. The options differ in *what* is ported and *for how long* the fork pays.

<Columns>
  <Column label="Re-platform (recommended, staged)">
    **Base:** `upstream/main` including V2 and Pi V2. Loom's layer re-expressed as a V2 extension per the area verdicts.

    **Cost:** the textual merge is about two-thirds of pull 7; the port is the bulk — roughly 22,000 non-test lines of Loom orchestration server code move, of which the self-contained workers (dispatcher, fan-in, liveness, sweeps, libs, handlers, about 60 percent) re-seam with logic intact, the substrate (contract sidecar, decider arm, projections, shell join, about 25 percent) is rewritten against V2 shapes, and the driver re-anchoring and web re-hang are the rest. Expect several times pull 7's six sessions, spread across parallel tracks.

    **Risk:** V2 is 155 commits young and `Orchestrator.ts` is actively churning (32 upstream commits touched `orchestration-v2/` since V2 landed), so Loom's hunks there will conflict on every future pull — minimised by keeping Loom in the arm and the sidecar. Silent-failure risks are enumerated in the phase sketch.

    **Irreversible:** the `statev2.sqlite` cut-over (upstream keeps `state.sqlite` as a V1 rollback source, but Loom data written after cut-over is V2-only); the pi bump; the tool-transport change for every role text if names change.

    **Loom gives up:** the goal's event history, in-place rollback, the V1-era launch workarounds, `origin`/`controlPayload`, the REST transport, the V1 Pi driver.
  </Column>
  <Column label="Retain">
    **Base:** Loom's V1 engine and Pi driver stay; upstream's server orchestration is never merged again; web, mobile, client-runtime and usage drift are cherry-picked.

    **Cost now:** low for the server. But the cherry-pick premise fails: 47 of the 155 commits touch `ChatView`, `MessagesTimeline`, `Sidebar*`, `DiffPanel`, `ChatComposer` and the model picker, all of which now consume V2 `turnItems` and `OrchestrationV2ThreadShell`; `packages/client-runtime` state is V2-shaped; `/ws` rejects a client without `orchestrationProtocol: 2`. Retaining V1 therefore freezes the web client at pre-V2 too, and the store mobile app (2.0.0, protocol 2) stops connecting to a Loom server.

    **Risk:** compounding. Every provider adapter, settle/wake fix, PR watch, scheduled task and future feature is unreachable; Loom owns the pi driver alone against pi 1.x. Upstream becomes a source of ideas only.

    **Irreversible:** nothing today; the cost is the growing distance, which makes a later re-platform strictly harder than this one.

    **Loom gives up:** being a fork. This is the honest name for the option: stop syncing.
  </Column>
  <Column label="Hybrid — two engines side by side">
    **Base:** upstream for everything outside orchestration, provider and contracts; V1 kept alive beside V2 for Loom's layer while it is ported.

    **Cost:** the port plus the cost of keeping two deciders, two event stores (`orchestration_events` v1 and v2 in one file), two shell contracts and two Pi drivers compiling and consistent during the gap — and the web cannot render V1 threads under V2 contracts without a shim.

    **Risk:** every bug has two homes; the shim is precisely the dual-shape coexistence Carl's standing preferences forbid, and it tends to become permanent.

    **Verdict:** rejected as an end state or an interim. The *staging* benefit it promises — not losing Loom's features during the port — is achieved instead by keeping **production** on pre-pull-9 Loom while the integration branch is V2-only, with a feature freeze on Loom's orchestration layer until cut-over. Nothing V1 runs on the pull-9 branch at any point.
  </Column>
</Columns>

<Callout tone="decision">
**Recommendation: staged re-platform.** It is the only option under which Loom's thesis — a durable, inspectable organisation of threads the *system* keeps coherent, attributable and recoverable — keeps getting the substrate it needs from upstream (adapters, restart reconciliation, settle/wake, a tool bridge every provider shares) while Loom spends its effort on the workflow layer upstream has explicitly chosen not to build. The end state is smaller than today: the V1 engine, the V1 Pi driver, the REST transport, the goal aggregate, the launch workarounds and several columns go, and what remains sits on seams upstream has now documented as the sanctioned way for a fork to extend V2 (a closed union extended beside it; a separate migration ledger). Correctness over convenience says: pay the port once, cleanly, rather than carry two engines or stop syncing.
</Callout>

Pull 8 is upstream up to `024d49520e` — the commit before V2 — merged onto Loom, and it is exactly the merge base the trial merge used. ### Phase 0 — land pull 8

### Phase 1 — mechanical merge, upstream wins on structure

Merge `upstream/main` with `merge.renameLimit=30000`. Resolve the 155 textual conflicts with the pull-7 tooling, choosing the V2 world wherever a file is where upstream wired V2 in (`ws.ts`, `server.ts`, `serverRuntimeStartup.ts`, `client-runtime/src/state/*`, `ChatView.tsx`). Take upstream's deletion on all 95 modify/delete files. Move the 86 relocated Loom files **out** of `orchestration-v2/` into a tsconfig-excluded quarantine directory so they are diffable during the port and deleted in phase 4 — never compiled. ### Phase 2 — substrate

`orchestrationV2.loom.ts` (Loom fields on `AppThread` and `ThreadShell`, commands, events, enums); the guard arm in `Orchestrator.ts` and `Orchestrator.loom.ts`; the hunk cluster in `message.dispatch` (turn-start rules, supersede, `start_if_idle`), `run.interrupt`, archive/unarchive/delete cascades, `thread.auto-settle` blockers, metadata rename; receipt-on-zero-events if V2 lacks it; Loom migrations creating the `loom_*` sidecar tables; the Loom projector and shell-query join. ### Phase 3 — control plane, tools, driver, web (four parallel tracks)

**3a** Loom MCP toolkit and handlers; `orchestration` capability withheld for Loom sessions; Loom's extension (profile fetch, `enable_toolset`, prompt debug, search guard); `ask_user_question` on V2 runtime requests. **3b** Dispatcher, fan-in, provisioner (via `defer_start` worktree strategy), liveness sweep with heartbeat from the V2 stream, exhaustion resume, handoff drafter, reaper — re-seamed on `OrchestratorV2`. **3c** Failover, retry tier, cost attribution, quotas, sanitiser re-anchored on `agent_settled`. **3d** Web surfaces re-hung on the V2 shell; `ControlDigestCard` on `notification`; goal shell-stream items. **Gate — the real Pi workstream smoke test**, run on a copied database with the dev-verify recipe: an orchestrator scaffolds a coder with an isolated worktree and a gated reviewer attached to it; the coder submits, the reviewer returns `needs_rework`, the loop runs to `clean` without waking the orchestrator; fan-in merges into the parent tree; the parent is woken once with a digest naming the report path; a second child raises `needs_guidance` and its dependent does not start; the server is restarted mid-run and the child resumes; a child with a frozen heartbeat trips the stall nudge; a `consult_thread` against a child whose worktree has been reaped answers. **Silent failures to design against.** (1) The database copy: every Loom table arrives inert and nothing complains — only the Loom importer and the board make the loss visible. (2) Session identity: a wrong lookup creates an empty same-named session and the thread forgets everything, with no error. (3) The pi bump: a regenerated patch that applies to `dist/` but not the minified bundle passes typecheck and fails at runtime. (4) `Orchestrator.ts` hunks: the next upstream pull will conflict here every time; keep them few and marked. (5) `rerere`: the trial's preimages are in the shared cache without postimages, so nothing auto-resolves — do not expect it to. (6) The 117 silently auto-merged files, eight of which lost an exported name; `lostdecls.py` is the check.

`/home/Carl/.t3/cockpit/worktrees/loom/t3code-87358b97/plans/upstream-pull9-strategy/plan.mdx` — committed on `t3code/plan-next-upstream-merge` as `9ef622bed5` (only that file staged). Render gate (`lint-plan.mjs`) passes with no findings: 12 area cards each with a `ReviewChoice`, a verdict table, a collisions table, a three-column mechanism comparison, a Mermaid phase graph, a gate checklist, and a nine-question `QuestionForm`. Carl records decisions in-app; nothing is pending on me.

### The recommendation, in one paragraph (for Carl)

**Re-platform, staged.** Take `upstream/main` including Orchestration V2 and the Pi V2 adapter as the base, and re-express Loom's layer as a V2 extension: Loom's thread fields/commands/events as a sidecar contract on V2's store; Loom's decider rules as one delegation guard arm plus about six marked hunks in upstream's decider (the same pattern Loom used on V1); the control-plane workers (dispatcher, fan-in, liveness, exhaustion resume) re-seamed onto V2's `streamDomainEvents`/`getShellSnapshot`/`dispatch` (which I verified exist, and V2 adds the replay-from-sequence V1 lacked); Loom's agent tools moved off bespoke REST routes onto upstream's MCP bridge as a Loom toolkit, with upstream's `delegate_task` family **withheld** from Loom threads so there is one delegation model per prompt. The evidence says upstream is heading to the same destination as Loom on the *substrate* (durable children as real threads, event-sourced commands with receipts, durable outbox, restart reconciliation, shared tool bridge, and — notably — upstream now explicitly endorses the separate fork migration ledger Loom already has) and to a different or absent destination on the *workflow* (no plan axis, dependencies, gates, goals, human holds, liveness, per-child worktree). Adopt the substrate, retain the workflow. "Retain V1" is not cheap: upstream rewired web/mobile/client-runtime around V2 contracts and gates `/ws` on protocol 2, so it freezes the whole client and disconnects the store mobile app — it is "stop syncing". Two engines side by side is rejected as dual-shape; the staging is instead a feature freeze on Loom's orchestration layer with production staying on pre-pull-9 Loom until a real Pi workstream smoke test passes. **Pull 8 should land first** (it is the exact trial-merge base; folding or abandoning it re-does or wastes its 12 resolutions).

### Verdicts most likely to surprise Carl

1. **Drop Loom's 2,959-line Pi driver for upstream's `PiAdapterV2`**, keeping ~1,500 lines of Loom economics (failover/retry tier, cost attribution, quotas, bundled patched pi, sanitiser) as hunks — the failover logic must be *re-anchored* on `agent_settled`, not ported. Session identity resolves in upstream's favour: `nativeThreadRef` is the authority, `--session-id <threadId>` at first launch keeps the file recognisable, the ~10 name-based consumers re-point, and patch 0001 is extended to RPC `switch_session` (pi already accepts `cwdOverride` there). Pi bumps to 1.0.2.
2. **Several Loom mechanisms were V1 workarounds V2 makes unnecessary — verify, then delete:** stuck-launch CAS repair, `turn-start.fail`, the pending-steer stash, `notify_thread`'s durable defer queue (V2 queues server-side), the three-layer `ask_user_question` settlement (V2 `RuntimeRequest` with `not_resumable`), message `origin`/`controlPayload` columns (V2's `notification{source,outcome,summary,detail}` is the same twin), `pendingUserInputHeader/Since` columns, Loom's runtime-axis projection (V2 `activityRunStatus`), and worktree provisioning as a call site (V2's `defer_start` + `workspaceStrategy: worktree` + `prepared-run.release` is Loom's provision-at-promotion). Goals also lose the V2-incompatible `goal` aggregate and become plain Loom tables (open question, default yes).
3. **Loom children are *not* V2 delegated tasks.** `delegated_task.request` requires a live parent turn, publishes the first run's output as the stable result and never reopens — contradicting Loom's start gates and gate loops. Loom's spawn arm nests upstream's `thread.create` with `subagent` lineage (a nesting pattern upstream already uses), which also gives Loom upstream's sidebar filtering for free.
4. **One genuine engine-invariant hunk is unavoidable:** V2's `message.dispatch` has `queue_after_active` but no "defer if busy"; Loom's idle-only digest wakes need a `start_if_idle` dispatch mode (no-op-with-receipt when a run is live). Plus a check that V2 persists a receipt on zero-event success.

### Open questions for Carl (all in the bottom form, with defaults)

Overall mechanism (default: staged re-platform) · pull 8 (default: land first) · accept an orchestration feature freeze with production on today's Loom (default: yes) · bare vs `mcp__t3-code__`-prefixed tool names on the MCP bridge (default: bare, via a small hunk) · expose any of upstream's orchestration tools to Loom agents (default: none at first) · goal storage as plain tables vs event-sourced (default: tables) · historical import scope (default: all goals + task trees, workstream fields for non-archived threads only) · pi version (default: bump to 1.0.2, regenerate patches) · keep upstream's unsolicited-run kill guard (default: keep; audit pi-intercom).

### What the parent should act on

- Hand the document to Carl for in-app review; his `ReviewChoice`/`QuestionForm` answers ride his next turn.
- Once answered, a follow-on planner can write the phase-1/phase-2 implementation plans; the phase sketch names the gates (`vp check`, `vp run typecheck`, the Pi workstream smoke test with its concrete scenario, the ported `PiCwdOverride` contract test through `switch_session`) and the silent-failure traps (DB copy, session identity, patch bundle, `Orchestrator.ts` churn, `rerere` preimages, the 8 auto-merged files that lost exports).

sections.addendum:
<addendum>
You operate inside T3 Code's work model: Goals → Tasks → Workstream. This is how every thread here is organised, whatever its role.

A GOAL is a single durable objective that outlives any one session and spans many — the north star for all work under it. Orient to it; if work drifts from the goal, refocus or update it. A goal is decomposed into a TASK TREE: the living, shared record of what is done and what remains — for the agents working it and for the human who glances at it to re-orient. It is kept current as work progresses.

Work happens in a WORKSTREAM: a tree of durable threads. You are one thread in it, and your role overlay says how you act within it. A ROOT thread ORCHESTRATES — it plans, delegates, and reviews rather than doing the work by hand. A CHILD thread EXECUTES a single self-contained brief and hands a result back. A child is a real, persistent thread a human can open and talk to, not a throwaway: spawning one is deliberate, and a child starts fresh — it inherits none of the parent's conversation, only the brief it is given. Work flows down as briefs and back up as reports. The workstream is a graph of threads: dependencies are its edges, so dependent work waits while independent branches run in parallel (with bounded review-gate loops as the one deliberate cycle) — and the graph is not fixed; it is expected to be amended and replanned as understanding improves.

Getting information from another thread, cheapest first: a thread's REPORT is its curated hand-back — read that first. The workstream GRAPH lets you see every thread and find any of them without searching (`workstream_list`). To resolve an ambiguity, CONSULT the thread that holds the context. The full thread history can be accessed via the Pi session jsonl file if necessary.

A few principles keep this coherent:
- Your assignment is your task. For a child that is its spawn brief; at the root it is the user's direction. An inherited goal is background - align to it, but where it and your assignment differ, follow the assignment.
- Work at your level, and keep heavy sub-phases out of your context. If you orchestrate, delegate substantial work to children rather than absorbing it inline, and when new non-trivial work crystallises mid-conversation, pause to lay out or amend the graph before diving in. If you execute a brief, do it yourself rather than re-delegating it — but any thread, at any depth, may hand a bounded sub-phase of its own brief to a child when all three hold: the sub-phase is context-heavy; a short brief can carry everything it needs from you; and what comes back is an artefact — files on disk plus a short report — not understanding you must carry into later turns. Typical cases: a screenshot-capture pass, a large-corpus read, a bulk extraction. Done in situ, every page of that stays in your context for the rest of the thread; done by a child, it dies with the child. # Workstream State Model — Three-Axis Design

Status: **agreed intent** (design session, grill-me). This document pins the
intended state model for T3 Code Workstream threads. A separate implementation
plan and coder follow; this is the contract they build to.

Supersedes the single-`status` model in `.plans/phase-c-status-and-dependencies.md`
(effective-display precedence, permissive transitions) and refines the dispatcher
contract in `.plans/phase-d-core-dispatcher-design.md`.

---

## 1. Problem — one field, three meanings

Today a single stored `ThreadStatus` (`planned | running | blocked | review |
done | error`) conflates three orthogonal things, which is the root cause of the
observed misuse:

- **Plan intent** — where a node sits in the intended design (a lane an
  agent/human chooses).
- **Runtime condition** — whether the agent loop is literally executing a turn
  right now.
- **Attention** — whether a human is needed, and why.

Because they share one writable enum, they desync and get misused:

- `review` is told to a `coder` whose output flows to a separate `reviewer`
  thread — conflating "a *reviewer thread* will process this" (automatic) with
  "a *human* must review this" (pause). `review` was never defined for the
  thread, so it was used meaninglessly.
- `blocked` conflates "waiting on upstream work" (resolves itself) with "paused
  awaiting a human" (won't resolve without action).
- A node can read `running` while nothing executes, or execute while labelled
  otherwise — "describes the plan" and "is the truth" silently disagree.
- A re-engaged `done` node (a follow-up question beyond original scope) has no
  way to show *activity* without appearing to revert to incomplete.

The runtime overlay already half-exists on the read path
(`resolveBaseColumn`/`getEffectiveColumn` derive `running` from live
session/turn signals; `getEffectiveColumn` derives `blocked` from unmet
dependencies). The bug is that these derived facts share one vocabulary with —
and are overwritten by — the agent-writable stored field.

---

## 2. The model — three independent axes

State is decomposed into **three axes**. The slogan *"status describes the plan;
runtime is the truth"* becomes literally true because an agent can only ever
write plan/attention intent, never the runtime or the control-plane-owned
values.

### Axis 1 — Plan lane (intent; the kanban board)
======
### Axis 1 — Plan lane (intent; the kanban board)

Mutually-exclusive waypoints describing the node's intended position in the
design. This is the only "lifecycle" axis and it is deliberately small:

```
planned  →  ready  →  in_progress  →  done
                                  ↘  cancelled   (terminal, from any pre-terminal lane)
```

| lane | meaning |
|---|---|
| `planned` | in the plan, **staged/held** — not released to run |
| `ready` | **released** — will run once dependencies clear |
| `in_progress` | the active phase of the plan is underway |
| `done` | accepted-complete — **releases dependents** |
| `cancelled` | abandoned (was planned, deliberately stopped) — terminal, does **not** release dependents |

Everything that used to muddy the lane moves off it:

| old `status` value | where it lives now |
|---|---|
| `planned` / `done` | plan lane (unchanged) |
| `running` | split: plan lane `in_progress` (control-plane-set) + runtime `executing` (derived) |
| `blocked` (on upstream) | **derived** from unmet dependencies — never stored |
| `review` | **attention** reason = *awaiting acceptance* (plan stays `in_progress`) |
| `blocked` (paused on a human) | **attention** reason = *needs guidance* |
| `error` | **attention** reason = *failed/stalled* (system-set) |
| pending approval / user-input | **attention** reasons (already derived today) |

### Axis 2 — Runtime / activity (the truth; derived, never stored as intent)

A pure projection over the session and latest turn — *is a turn turning right
now?* Never an agent-writable field.

| runtime | derivation |
|---|---|
| `executing` | `session.status === "running"` or `latestTurn.state === "running"` |
| `starting` | session connecting / spinning up (transient) |
| `idle` | session exists, no active turn |
| (none) | no session yet |

Activity **bubbles up**: a subtree with any `executing` descendant reads as
active *regardless of plan state*. A re-engaged `done` node is `done` (plan) +
`executing` (activity) at once.

The only stored "activity-ish" value is the plan lane `in_progress`, whose sole
writer is the control plane at kickoff. There is nothing to keep in sync, so it
cannot desync.

### Axis 3 — Attention (needs-a-human; the single notification surface)

A reason-tagged flag that can co-exist with any plan lane and bubbles up. This is
the **one** axis the notification/escalation machinery watches.

| attention reason | raised by |
|---|---|
| `error` (failed / stalled / looping) | **system** (liveness sweep) |
| `awaiting_approval` | **system** (open approval request) |
| `awaiting_input` | **system** (open user-input request) |
| `awaiting_acceptance` (review/sign-off) | **agent** ("my output needs sign-off") |
| `needs_guidance` (stuck) | **agent** ("I can't proceed without a human") |

Attention is a union of **derived** reasons (error, approval, input) and
**agent-raised** reasons (acceptance, guidance). When the underlying condition
clears (the human answers, the plan advances to `done`/`cancelled`, the agent
resumes), the flag clears.

> Names above are the proposed wire contract. Australian-English prose is used
> throughout this document; identifiers stay conventional.

---

## 3. Two orthogonal start-gates

A thread starts executing only when **both** gates clear — and the two gates are
the same "waiting on work vs waiting on a human" split, applied at the launch
boundary:

1. **Dependency gate** (automatic, structural): every `blockedBy` thread is
   `done`. Waiting here ⇒ board shows **blocked (on upstream)**; resolves itself.
2. **Release gate** (intentional): plan lane is `ready`, not `planned`. Waiting
   here ⇒ the plan is **staged but unreleased**; needs a human/agent to release.

The dispatcher promotes when `lane == ready && deps satisfied && not started`
(today's trigger is just deps-satisfied — this adds the release gate).

`planned` is therefore a genuine **hold**: even with deps clear it sits still
until released. This enables laying out a whole DAG for human review of the work
breakdown *before any tokens are spent*.

**Release semantics:** releasing flips the whole subtree `planned → ready` at
once; dependency edges still sequence execution layer by layer.

**Spawn default:** a plain `workstream_spawn` defaults to `ready` (current
"spawn → it runs" ergonomics preserved). **Staging is the explicit opt-in**
(spawn `planned`), used for the review-the-graph flow.

---

## 4. Start / stop / re-engage

### Start ("execution drives status")

The dispatcher remains the **sole start authority**. On kickoff it sends the
first-turn prompt **and** sets plan lane → `in_progress` in one atomic
transaction (today's `setRunning`, retargeted). Runtime → `executing` follows
from the turn running. The act of starting writes `in_progress`; an agent never
does.

### `done` is sticky (activity ≠ plan)

A started turn pulls a **pre-completion** lane (`ready`, or `in_progress` with a
raised attention flag) to `in_progress`. It does **not** revert a terminal lane:

- Re-engaging a `done` node (out-of-scope follow-up) lights the **activity** axis
  only; the lane stays `done`. Reopening the plan requires an *explicit* lane
  change — implicit un-completing is the bug being removed.
- Answering an `awaiting_acceptance` thread (sending revision feedback) resumes

There is a mechanic to **stop** a running agent (`thread.turn.interrupt`
interrupts the active turn; runtime → `idle`). Restarting is typically just
sending a prompt (which progresses the next turn → `executing`).

**Invariant:** *a node that is not executing, will not be auto-resumed, and is
not plan-terminal (`done`/`cancelled`) must carry a raised attention flag.*
Nothing that needs a human may sit silently halted. The discriminator is "is
there an owner who will resume it?" — the same resolves-itself-vs-needs-a-human

I'm examining which lane values are truly load-bearing versus derivable. The "planned" hold state seems essential since nothing else encodes "don't start yet," while "ready" looks like it could just be derived from "not held and not started yet," even though it's stored for the dispatcher's convenience.

"in_progress" seems similarly derivable—just "has a run and not terminal"—existing mainly so a lane column can show activity without checking runtime state. "yielded" is trickier: it's a genuinely distinct control-plane state that blocks auto-settle, almost like the orchestrator's version of needing attention. "done" feels essential since it's the only way completion gets encoded through cooperative self-report, and "cancelled" is clearly a load-bearing terminal non-releasing state. That leaves held, done, cancelled, and yielded as the minimal necessary set, with ready and in_progress being derivable conveniences.

So the six-value lane looks partly vestigial, carrying over kanban-style visual columns from an older single status enum that the three-axis redesign mostly pruned but left intact. I'm now considering whether a leaner alternative—an outcome field, a held boolean, and a yielded flag—would simplify things further, collapsing the reversion rule and the kickoff write into something much simpler, and shrinking the lane-setting tool to just release, cancel, and done. That feels like a real improvement, more consistent with treating status as descriptive rather than authoritative, and I want to compare this against how V2 handles thread shell status as idle versus run status.

Looking at V2's fields, nothing there maps cleanly to plan completion, and its "settle" concept is explicitly a sidebar-visibility partition rather than control-plane logic, which rules it out as a stand-in for "done." I'm weighing the counter-arguments for keeping the lane anyway—agents and the board rely on it as shared vocabulary, and the stored in_progress value serves specific dispatcher functions like distinguishing started-once from never-started, feeding the brief-needed ladder and idle backstop—but under V2 that distinction becomes cheap to derive from whether runs exist, whereas under V1 it required a separate lookup.

The port is the natural moment to make this change since the lane becomes a Loom field on V2 either way, so reworking it now is cheaper than later, even though it widens an already large port's scope. I'm deciding to answer Carl directly in chat with a recommendation, then also capture this as a real open decision by adding a short paragraph and question to Area C of the document, since that keeps the decision in-app rather than buried in chat.

content.text:
Honest answer: it is **half load-bearing, half vestigial**, and the vestigial half is a residue of the single-`status` enum it replaced.

**Where it came from.** The original workstream had one writable `status` (`planned | running | blocked | review | done | error`) that conflated plan intent, runtime and "needs a human", and agents misused it (`.plans/workstream-state-model-design.md` §1). The three-axis redesign moved runtime to a derived projection and attention to its own flag — correct — but kept a six-value lane as "Axis 1 … the kanban board". The lane is literally what remained of the old enum after the other two axes were carved off.

**What each value actually does today:**

| Lane | Who writes it | Is it load-bearing? |
|---|---|---|
| `planned` | agent/human (`staged`, `set_lane`) | **Yes** — the only "don't start yet" hold. Nothing else encodes staging. |
| `ready` | agent/human (`release`) | **No** — derivable as *not held ∧ never started*. Stored only so the board has a column. |
| `in_progress` | control plane at kickoff | **No** — derivable as *has started ∧ not terminal*. The design doc itself calls it "the only stored activity-ish value". It exists so the lane column shows "underway" without consulting runtime — a display convenience that costs a transactional write on every kickoff, the "§7 unifying rule" (every turn start reverts `ready`/`yielded`), the sticky-terminal rule, and the `reopen` hunk in gates. |
| `yielded` | control plane from submit routing | **Yes, but it is misfiled** — "parked awaiting the orchestrator's decision" is semantically an *attention* flag whose audience is an agent rather than a human. It is not a position in the plan. |
| `done` | control plane from submit, or forced | **Yes** — completion is cooperative self-report, so something must record it. V2 has no equivalent (a run completing ≠ the work being accepted). This is the single most important bit in Loom's model: it releases dependents and triggers fan-in. |
| `cancelled` | agent/human | **Yes** — terminal, non-releasing. |

So the irreducible core is: a **hold** bit, a **terminal outcome** (`done | cancelled | null`), and a **yielded** flag. `ready` and `in_progress` are board columns stored as state.

**Is the implementation the best approach? No.** The smaller correct shape is `held: boolean` + `outcome: done | cancelled | null` + `yielded` moved into the attention set (as the agent-audience reason). Consequences: the atomic kickoff write disappears; §7 shrinks to "clear `yielded` on turn start"; sticky-terminal becomes trivially true; the gate `reopen` is just `outcome := null`; `workstream_set_lane` collapses to `release`/`cancel` (done already comes from `submit`); the board still shows five columns, derived (`held`, `waiting on deps`, `ready`, `in progress`, `done`) from fields that cannot desync. Under V2 "has started" is `runs.length > 0` on the thread projection, which is exactly the cheap signal V1 lacked — one reason the stored `in_progress` felt necessary before.

**My recommendation:** decide this now, because the lane becomes a Loom field on V2 in phase 2 and that contract is the hard-to-reverse part; implementing it then is nearly free compared with carrying the enum across and redesigning later. The counter-argument is scope on an already large port, and that agents currently reason in lane vocabulary via `workstream_list` — but the rendered text can keep saying "in progress" regardless of storage.

I'll add this to the document as an open question (default: collapse to hold + outcome + yielded-as-attention) with a short note in Area C, so you can record it in-app rather than in chat.
