## Area D — Review gates and verdict routing

**Same destination? No.** Upstream has nothing structural — no gate, verdict, round, cap or reviewer binding. Its guidance is the opposite design: re-call `delegate_task` per round with the prior findings, a fresh reviewer session each time, and never continue a review on `childThreadId` (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §D). Loom's design is a first-class, outcome-conditional loop edge in the graph that runs coder → reviewer → coder to resolution **without waking the orchestrator**, round-capped, with yield-to-orchestrator as the default for anything unexpected (`docs/design/workstream-review-gates.md`).

**Verdict — retain Loom, re-expressed on V2.** `routes`, `gateRounds`, `pendingRework`, `lastOutcome`, `reportPath` are Loom fields; `thread.work.submit` and gate traversal are Loom commands in the arm; `routeWorkSubmit` (`packages/shared/src/workstreamGraph.ts`, 576 lines, pure) is untouched. The one V1 hunk this area needed — `reopen` on `thread.turn.start` reverting a `done` coder to `in_progress` atomically — disappears as a hunk: the gate-traverse arm emits the Loom lane event and nests the `message.dispatch` in one transaction, the same way the spawn arm nests `thread.create`. Per-round report files, deterministic `server:workstream-gate:<R>:<round>:<leg>` ids, the raise-then-complete refusal (10 of 20 audited raises had been erased by their own submit), the bypass guard on a self-issued `set_lane done`, and the suppressions (`isWaitingInGate`, `isMemberOfUnresolvedGate`) all port with the dispatcher.

**Users gain** nothing from upstream here; the review-round guidance in upstream's shared instructions is not injected into Loom threads (Area B). **Users lose** nothing.

**Cost class — port.**

<Card id="area-d-card" heading="Area D verdict — retain on V2" tone="accent" badge="RETAIN ON V2" meta={["port", "reopen hunk becomes a nested dispatch", "routeWorkSubmit unchanged"]}>
  <ReviewChoice itemId="area-d" label="D · Review gates and verdict routing" />
</Card>

## Area E — Goals and task tree

**Same destination? Upstream has nothing.** No durable objective above a thread, no shared tree, no agent tool to read or edit one. Upstream's adjacent things — per-run todo lists, proposed plans, scheduled tasks, the parent's `Subagent` rows — are not goals (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §E).

**Verdict — retain Loom as-is, with one simplification: goals and tasks as plain Loom tables, not a V2 aggregate.** Under V1 the goal was an aggregate kind in the shared event store with its own stream because the V1 read model folded the whole log from sequence 0 on boot and the goal needed to survive that. V2's projections are SQL tables maintained by a projector, and V2's event table is keyed by `thread_id`; a goal has no thread. Giving the goal a place in V2's log means either a Loom-added column on upstream's events table or a parallel Loom event table — both are ceremony for a record whose history nobody replays. The smaller correct end state is `loom_goals` and `loom_goal_tasks` written directly by the goal tool handlers (with `clientRequestId` idempotency at the toolkit edge, which upstream's MCP layer already provides via `stableCommandId`), and the shell-stream `goal-upserted` / `goal-removed` items broadcast from the handler. The task-tree libs (`goalTaskTree.ts`, `goalTaskMarkdown.ts` round-trip identity, `goalTaskRender.ts`, the 300-character register cap, anchors with branch scoping, the echo-after-every-mutation) are unchanged. This is recorded as an open question because it is a real design choice the evidence does not settle.

The hooks Loom needs from the engine are the same four as today and land as hunks in V2's decider: `project.delete` refuses or cascades active goals; archiving a goal's last active thread archives the goal (and unarchive reverses); renaming the sole thread renames the goal; attaching a goal to a thread attaches it to goal-less descendants. The emergent goal (side-channel generation on turn 1 or 2) rides V2's effect outbox as a Loom effect kind beside `thread-title.generate`. Prompt injection is Area G. `goal_handoff` and `goal_continue` create staged roots and siblings through the Loom spawn arm.

**Users gain** nothing from upstream; **users lose** the goal's event history (which no surface reads).

**Cost class — port, smaller afterwards.**

<Card id="area-e-card" heading="Area E verdict — retain as-is, goals as plain tables" tone="neutral" badge="RETAIN" meta={["port", "goal aggregate dropped", "4 cascade hunks"]}>
  <ReviewChoice itemId="area-e" label="E · Goals and task tree" placeholder="Reject here only if goals must stay event-sourced; the storage question is also in the bottom form." />
</Card>

## Area F — Context transfer

**Same destination? Partly.** Upstream made transfers explicit, auditable artefacts (`ContextTransfer`, `ContextHandoff`; README invariants 8–9 "not hidden prompt hacks"), gave agents `t3_thread_send` (agent → thread, `senderThreadId`, `createdBy:"agent"`, never interrupts, `auto` → steer or queue), `t3_thread_read` with incremental paging, and `thread.fork` with lazy native resolution for pi. Loom's "cheapest first" ladder — report, `workstream_list`, frozen-fork `consult_thread`, then the session jsonl — has no upstream counterpart for the report and the consult.

**Verdict — hybrid.**

- **`notify_thread` → V2 `message.dispatch` with `senderThreadId`.** Same destination. Loom's rules stay as handler policy: the ordered-pair hourly cap, refusal to re-engage a terminal or archived target, relationship-aware framing. Loom's orchestration-layer **durable defer queue** was a V1 workaround for "never interrupt, deliver when idle"; V2's `queue_after_active` queues durably server-side, so the queue is deleted.
- **Control-plane messages → V2 `notification`.** Loom stamped `origin ∈ {human, kickoff, orchestrator, control_notice, notify}` and a `controlPayload` on messages (two migrations, two columns) so digest / yield / gate-resolution / notify arrivals render as cards. V2's `message.dispatch` carries `notification:{source, outcome, summary, detail}` and `createdBy`, which is the same twin. Adopt it; extend the closed `source` enum with Loom's values (one-line contract hunk); `ControlDigestCard` reads `notification`. The `origin` / `control_payload_json` columns go.
- **Result delivery to the parent** — collision, resolved by Area A: because Loom children are not V2 delegated tasks, the dispatcher's terminal-child rail composes the wake (`notification` with summary and the report's absolute path, coalesced into digests, `start_if_idle`) and nothing ever points the parent at `task_status`.
- **Reports and `workstream_list`** — retain; `reportPath` is a Loom field, the report file lives under the durable state dir as today.
- **`consult_thread`** — retain as-is; it is a throwaway `pi --mode rpc --fork` outside the adapter, read-only tools, Q&A recorded on the asker (`thread.consult.record` in the arm; the consult card's activity-payload survival becomes a turn-item hunk). It depends on locating the target's session file — Area L.
- **`thread_fork`, `/handoff`, `/retro`** → V2 `thread.fork` (idle thread, `fork` lineage, pending transfer resolved as `native_fork` for pi at first dispatch) plus Loom's drafter reactor and composer intercepts retained. Same destination, smaller Loom code.
- **Steering durability** — see Area C; deleted.

**Users gain** upstream's Lineage panel showing Loom's forks and transfers, and `t3_thread_transfers`-style auditability. **Users lose** nothing visible.

**Cost class — port, with four deletions.**

<Card id="area-f-card" heading="Area F verdict — hybrid" tone="warning" badge="HYBRID" meta={["port", "notify queue, origin/controlPayload, steer stash: delete", "consult retained"]}>
  <ReviewChoice itemId="area-f" label="F · Context transfer" />
</Card>

## Area G — Prompt composition

**Same destination? Partly.** Upstream injects shared text into pi through the extension's `before_agent_start` and gives pi no per-thread prompt (`acceptsSystemContext:false`; `03-pi-driver-comparison.md` §3). Loom composes, per thread, the work-model addendum, thread-identity clause, role overlay, shipping policy, role catalogue, goal context and relocation clause, and passes it as `--append-system-prompt` argv so the launch bytes are captured as identity and a `forkFrom` child replays them for a byte-identical cache prefix.

**Verdict — retain what Loom composes; re-express how it is delivered.** The composition moves from the deleted `ProviderCommandReactor.startProviderSession` to a Loom hook where V2 opens sessions (`ProviderSessionManager`), producing the same text. Delivery: a Loom field on `ProviderAdapterV2OpenSessionInput` (`appendSystemPrompt`, `skills`, `extensions`) that `buildPiRpcLaunch` turns into `--append-system-prompt`, `--skill` and the second `--extension`. The alternative — fetching the prompt in the extension's `before_agent_start` — is rejected because it adds a network step to every session start and breaks the argv-identity property `forkFrom` relies on. Role overlays, kickoff wrapper, ship policy, skills catalogue, control-plane notice copy and the prompt-debug sidecar are self-contained and move as-is.

**Users gain** nothing from upstream (its `RuntimeInstructions` are not sent to pi). **Users lose** nothing.

**Cost class — port** (one contract field, one launch hunk, the session-open hook).

<Card id="area-g-card" heading="Area G verdict — retain composition, new delivery seam" tone="accent" badge="RETAIN ON V2" meta={["port", "open-session input field", "argv identity preserved"]}>
  <ReviewChoice itemId="area-g" label="G · Prompt composition" />
</Card>

## Area H — Model selection

**Same destination? Partly.** Both resolve a child's model at spawn against the live registry and fail on an unavailable instance or model (`resolveTarget` upstream; `resolveSpawnModelSelection` in Loom). Upstream resolves by *name* with capability constraints; Loom resolves a *task shape* (`explore | thorough | mechanical`) against an operator capability matrix and usage headroom so the parent never names a model.

**Verdict — retain Loom's resolution; adopt V2's records and upstream's thinking ladder.** The resolution is engine-independent and stays at the toolkit edge, writing V2's thread `modelSelection`; each V2 `Run` records its own `providerInstanceId` and `modelSelection`, which is better than Loom's single stored selection for attribution. Adopt upstream's per-model thinking ladder (option id `thinking`, `off…max`, default from pi's settings) and migrate stored `thinkingLevel` selections in a Loom migration — a collision resolved in upstream's favour because the ladder is derived from pi's model metadata and Loom's was one global list. Keep `PI_DEFAULT_MODEL` as the default (hunk) rather than upstream's "Pi default" sentinel, because Loom pins the session model at birth for failover. Failover and exhaustion are Area L.

**Cost class — trivial plus a data migration.**

<Card id="area-h-card" heading="Area H verdict — retain resolution, adopt records" tone="warning" badge="HYBRID" meta={["trivial", "thinkingLevel → thinking migration"]}>
  <ReviewChoice itemId="area-h" label="H · Model selection" />
</Card>

## Area I — Human-in-the-loop

**Same destination? Partly.** V2's `RuntimeRequest` (approvals, `user_input_request` with `header`, `question`, `options`, `multiSelect`, `allowCustomAnswer`, status `pending | resolved | expired | cancelled`, `responseCapability live | message | not_resumable`), `thread.user-input.dismiss`, and agent-answered questions are richer than Loom's broker over V1 activities. V2 has **no** acceptance or guidance hold and no agent tool to raise one (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md` §I).

**Verdict — adopt V2's request substrate; retain Loom's holds and shaping.**

- `ask_user_question` stays a Loom tool (1–4 validated questions, 2–4 options, one `recommended`, markdown body with file chips — richer than pi's `ctx.ui.select`). Its handler creates a V2 `user_input_request` on the calling thread with `responseCapability:"message"` and awaits its `runtime-request.updated` resolution, instead of Loom's in-memory long-poll broker. V2's `not_resumable` / `expired` handling after restart and manual-settle dismissal replace Loom's three-layer durable settlement (`userInputSettlement.ts`, 343 lines) — **verify** the 22-hour wedge case is covered, then delete.
- `thread.user-input.dismiss` exists in V2 under the same name; Loom's command goes.
- **Supersede** (a plain human message while a question is open resolves it `superseded` and is delivered as the tool result, withholding the turn start) → part of the `message.dispatch` hunk cluster in Area C.
- **Attention holds** (Area C) and the orchestrator doctrine "a child's `awaiting_acceptance` is a human hold" are retained; dependents stay blocked while a raise stands.
- Arrival surfaces: Loom's `pendingUserInputHeader / Since` columns are derived from V2's `pendingRuntimeRequest` on the shell; the columns and migration 1044 go. The panel additions and the MDX `QuestionForm` / `ReviewChoice` answer path are web-only and unchanged.

**Users gain** approvals (V2 permission modes through the bridge's `tool_call` hook, if Loom ever runs below full-access) and upstream's pending-request panels. **Users lose** nothing.

**Cost class — port, with deletions.**

<Card id="area-i-card" heading="Area I verdict — adopt requests, retain holds" tone="warning" badge="HYBRID" meta={["port", "broker + settlement: delete after verification", "holds preserved"]}>
  <ReviewChoice itemId="area-i" label="I · Human-in-the-loop" />
</Card>

## Area J — UI

**Same destination? Yes for the chrome, partly for orchestration surfaces.** Loom already adopted upstream's flat sidebar V2 wholesale and attaches at its data seams (`docs/upstream-sync/23-sidebar-v2-rehome.md`). Upstream's Lineage panel, subagent cards, Working section and settle/wake sweep overlap Loom's active strip and rollups partially; nothing upstream renders a plan lane, a dependency edge, a gate round, a goal or a task tree.

**Verdict — adopt upstream UI wholesale; retain Loom's modules on the V2 shell.** The 56 conflicted web files and 12 mobile files are pull-7-shaped textual work; the real task is re-hanging Loom's surfaces — workstream board, fork–join graph, timeline, active strip, goal panel, control-plane cards, consult and handoff rows, thread tabs, usage chips, thread search, and the MDX plan/recap renderer (46 files, untouched) — on `OrchestrationV2ThreadShell` carrying `LoomThreadShellFields` and on V2's `OrchestrationV2ShellStreamItem` union extended with Loom's goal items. Loom's runtime rollup reads V2's `activityRunStatus` instead of projecting over V1 session + turn. Upstream's Lineage panel will show Loom children (they carry `subagent` lineage); keep both surfaces at first and prune duplication after the smoke test rather than deciding blind.

**Users gain** everything upstream shipped in 53 web/desktop and 13 mobile commits (settle/wake sweep, virtualised palette, mermaid, Working section, mobile 2.0). **Users lose** nothing; mobile never rendered Loom's workstream.

**Cost class — port.**

<Card id="area-j-card" heading="Area J verdict — adopt chrome, retain Loom surfaces" tone="info" badge="ADOPT + RETAIN" meta={["port", "shell contract re-hang", "MDX renderer untouched"]}>
  <ReviewChoice itemId="area-j" label="J · UI" />
</Card>

## Area K — Persistence

**Same destination? Yes.** Upstream's `legacy-orchestration-migration.md` now states what Loom's `22-migration-lane-split-plan.md` decided a year earlier: a fork's schema belongs in a separate migration table. Loom's `loom_sql_migrations` ledger at `1001+` is exactly that, and the trial merge confirmed the payoff — upstream's `Migrations.ts` conflicts on one trivial hunk, upstream's divergence warning and preview reconciler only scan `effect_sql_migrations`.

**Verdict — adopt V2's store, projections, outbox and `statev2.sqlite`; retain Loom's lane, re-targeted at Loom sidecar tables; Loom writes its own one-shot importer.** Loom's about 35 columns leave `projection_threads` (a V1 table that becomes dead) and land in `loom_thread_workstream` keyed by the V2 thread id, joined into the shell query — no `ALTER TABLE` on upstream's `orchestration_v2_projection_*` tables, so upstream's schema stays byte-identical. `projection_goals / goal_tasks / heartbeats / consults / peer_messages / usage_ledger` and the thread-search index move to `loom_*` names (or stay, if the migrator can rename cheaply). Loom's V1 event types stay in `orchestration_events` at `application_event_version = 1`, unread — Loom data is projection-table-driven under V2, not replayed.

edits.newText:
**Verdict — adopt V2's `RuntimeRequest` as the question record and panel; a Loom command creates it and a `runtime-request.respond` hunk routes the answer; retain Loom's holds and shaping.** This is a redesign, not a port, because the mechanism the obvious reading suggests does not exist and the nearest one would answer twice:

- **No V2 command creates a runtime request.** The command union has only `runtime-request.respond`; requests are born from adapter events (`handleExtensionUiRequest` for pi dialogs). So `ask_user_question` (1–4 validated questions, 2–4 options, one `recommended`, markdown body with file chips — richer than pi's `ctx.ui.select`) needs a Loom command, `runtime-request.create`, in the decider arm that emits `runtime-request.updated` with `kind: user_input` and a Loom marker on the request. That gives the request V2's panel, `pendingRuntimeRequest` on the shell, mobile's card, and `t3_pending_request_respond`.
- **V2's `respond` on a `message`-capability request dispatches the answers as a new user message** with `queue_after_active` (`Orchestrator.ts:6943–6980`). If Loom's tool handler also returned them as the tool result, the agent would receive the answer twice — exactly the double execution the supersede rule exists to prevent. So a hunk in the `runtime-request.respond` case: for a Loom-marked request with a *live* tool waiter, hand the answer to the waiter (Loom's extension long-poll returns it as the tool result) and emit no message; with no live waiter (the pi process died, server restarted) fall through to V2's own message delivery. That fall-through is what Loom's three-layer durable settlement (`userInputSettlement.ts`, 343 lines) was built to approximate on V1, so the settlement module is deleted once the hunk exists — the 22-hour wedge is covered by V2's request lifecycle plus the fall-through.
- `thread.user-input.dismiss` exists in V2 under the same name but **refuses** anything other than a `message`-capability `user_input` request ("This question needs an answer. Answer it or stop the turn.", `:7058`). Loom-created requests are `message`-capability, so dismiss works and Loom's command goes.

**The dangerous step, in three parts.** `initializeV2Database` copies `state.sqlite` to `statev2.sqlite` once, so every Loom table arrives intact and inert; upstream's `LegacyV1ThreadImporter` reads a fixed column list and none of Loom's. A Loom import step runs after upstream's, reading the copied V1 Loom tables and writing `loom_*` rows for whatever scope Carl chooses (open question; default: all goals and task trees, plus workstream fields for non-archived threads only — finished workstreams stay as inert rows, queryable by SQL).

1. **Session identity must be imported, or every Loom thread forgets everything.** Upstream's importer deliberately does not translate provider session identity: an imported thread has no provider thread, and its first continuation opens a *fresh* pi session with at most a 32,000-character transcript handoff (`docs/internals/legacy-orchestration-migration.md`, "First continuation"). For Loom that is amnesia on every live orchestrator and child that is continued, notified, woken or re-engaged after cut-over, and `consult_thread`, `forkFrom`, `goal_continue` and relocation lose their target because there is no `nativeThreadRef` to resolve. V2 also requires a strong native ref before restart continuation applies. So the Loom importer, for every imported thread with a pi session on disk, creates the V2 provider-thread binding with `nativeThreadRef` = the existing `*_<threadId>.jsonl` path and `strength: "strong"` — `thread.create.importedNativeThread{ref:{driver, nativeId, strength}}` already exists for exactly this (`orchestrationV2.ts:2493`). The phase-4 gate **continues a pre-existing imported thread and checks that it remembers**.
2. **The receipt ledger is not migrated.** V1's `server:` receipts stay in V1's table; after import, Loom's deterministic ids for already-delivered episodes (terminal-child digests, gate legs, brief-needed rungs) have no V2 receipt. Left alone, the dispatcher's first pass would either re-fire a burst of stale digests at every live parent or never fire. Resolution: Loom data is projection-driven under V2 and imported threads carry **no Loom events**, so the episode-keyed rails (keyed by a Loom event id) have nothing to fire for them by construction; the importer additionally stamps imported terminal children as notified so the delta rail treats them as history. Suppress, not seed.
3. **The copy happens only when `statev2.sqlite` is absent** (`initializeV2Database.ts:26`). If production is rolled back to V1 after a cut-over and later re-cut, V2 resumes from the stale first snapshot and silently loses everything V1 wrote in between. Delete `statev2.sqlite` before any second cut-over; the runbook step says so explicitly.

About 50 tracked files name `state.sqlite` (scripts, the `AGENTS.md` test-data recipe, the `test-t3-app` skill) and must follow.

**Verdict — adopt upstream's adapter; retain Loom's economics and operations as hunks and sidecar modules; resolve session identity in upstream's favour with a deterministic first file name.**

Adopted with the adapter: `agent_settled` + idle-probe turn settlement, extension dialogs → approvals and questions, native non-destructive rollback via `fork(entryId)`, native fork and fork-from-turn, `readThreadSnapshot` for handoffs, per-model thinking, live usage, the retry and compaction rows, the unsolicited-activity guard, `set_session_name`, `$skill` expansion.

Retained as Loom hunks or modules (sizes from report 03's list): bundled patched pi resolution and manual-only maintenance (`pi update --self` disabled); `--session-id <threadId>` at first launch; Loom open-session fields → argv (Area G); quota failover, tier-2 effective-model resolution, `model.rerouted`, the T3 slow-retry tier and `quota_exhausted` for the resume sweep — **re-anchored on `agent_settled`, not ported** (about 600 interleaved lines, the largest single item); cost and model attribution on usage (`costUsd` has no slot in V2 `tokenUsage` — a contract hunk); the codex → Anthropic tool-id sanitiser; account quota pollers; `PI_CACHE_RETENTION`; `queue_update` display. Stdout backpressure and `rawInput` merging are kept only if a measurement under V2 shows they are still needed.

**Session identity — the deepest collision.** Upstream's identity is the session file *path* (`nativeThreadRef`), resumed by RPC `switch_session`, rolled back by `fork(entryId)` which creates a new file; Loom's is a deterministic `*_<threadId>.jsonl`, resumed by patched `--session <file> --cwd`, rolled back by in-place truncation, and about ten Loom modules locate sessions by that name. Two identity schemes is dual-shape; the resolution is: the first launch passes `--session-id <threadId>` so the file is still recognisable by name and `$PI_SESSION_FILE` (pi-native) still works for the identity clause, but **`nativeThreadRef` on the V2 provider thread is the authority**, and the ten consumers (`workstreamAsk`, `threadResolve`, `stallContext`, `workstreamLaunchIdentity`, the dispatcher, the fork and handoff handlers, the drafters) resolve the file through it. Rollback follows upstream (new file, ref updated). Patch 0001 is **extended to RPC `switch_session`** (pi's `switchSession` already accepts `cwdOverride`; the RPC handler just never passes it) so resume after a reaped worktree keeps working through upstream's resume path; the `PiCwdOverride` contract test is ported to that path.

**`forkFrom` (acknowledge-then-fork).** Upstream's `forkThread` forks natively in a throwaway process but does not replay launch identity, so the cache-prefix guarantee needs Loom's identity sidecar on top: retain `workstreamLaunchIdentity.ts` and replay argv in the Loom launch hunk when `forkFromThreadId` is set.

**Pi version.** Upstream recommends pi 1.0 and recorded fixtures on 1.0.0; Loom pins 0.99.2 with two patches. Both patches are still needed against 1.0.2 (`--cwd` absent, `auth.json` still written non-atomically). Default: bump to 1.0.2 and regenerate the patch bundle, because the adapter was written and tested against 1.0 behaviour.

**`PiSettings` collisions**: `enabled` default `false` upstream vs `true` in Loom (keep Loom's — Pi-first); `binaryPath:"pi"` resolves the global binary upstream vs the bundled patched copy in Loom (keep Loom's); `customModels` as objects upstream vs strings in Loom (adopt upstream's shape, migrate); the pi-only registry (one hunk, unchanged).

**Users gain** robustness (settlement, rollback, dialogs, fixtures) and the end of a 2,959-line driver Loom maintained alone. **Users lose** in-place rollback (fine — upstream's is non-destructive) and must accept a pi bump.

**Cost class — redesign-sized port.** The adapter is free; the re-anchoring of failover/retry and the identity re-pointing are the risk, and the latter fails *silently* (amnesia) when wrong, so it gets its own contract test.

## Overall mechanism options

The measured surface is the same under every option: 155 textual conflicts that fit the pull-7 method, and a port of the orchestration, provider-adapter, projection-persistence and V1-contract areas because no `ours` or `theirs` side compiles. The options differ in *what* is ported and *for how long* the fork pays.

<Columns>
  <Column label="Re-platform (recommended, staged)">
    **Base:** `upstream/main` including V2 and Pi V2. Loom's layer re-expressed as a V2 extension per the area verdicts.

    **Cost:** the textual merge is about two-thirds of pull 7; the port is the bulk — roughly 22,000 non-test lines of Loom orchestration server code move, of which the self-contained workers (dispatcher, fan-in, liveness, sweeps, libs, handlers, about 60 percent) re-seam with logic intact, the substrate (contract sidecar, decider arm, projections, shell join, about 25 percent) is rewritten against V2 shapes, and the driver re-anchoring and web re-hang are the rest. Expect several times pull 7's six sessions, spread across parallel tracks.

    **Risk:** V2 is 155 commits young and `Orchestrator.ts` is actively churning (32 upstream commits touched `orchestration-v2/` since V2 landed), so Loom's hunks there will conflict on every future pull — minimised by keeping Loom in the arm and the sidecar. Silent-failure risks are enumerated in the phase sketch.

    **Irreversible:** the `statev2.sqlite` cut-over (upstream keeps `state.sqlite` as a V1 rollback source, but Loom data written after cut-over is V2-only); the pi bump; the tool-transport change for every role text if names change.

    **Loom gives up:** the goal's event history, in-place rollback, the V1-era launch workarounds, `origin`/`controlPayload`, the REST transport, the V1 Pi driver.
  </Column>
  <Column label="Retain">
    **Base:** Loom's V1 engine and Pi driver stay; upstream's server orchestration is never merged again; web, mobile, client-runtime and usage drift are cherry-picked.

    **Cost now:** low for the server. But the cherry-pick premise fails: 47 of the 155 commits touch `ChatView`, `MessagesTimeline`, `Sidebar*`, `DiffPanel`, `ChatComposer` and the model picker, all of which now consume V2 `turnItems` and `OrchestrationV2ThreadShell`; `packages/client-runtime` state is V2-shaped; `/ws` rejects a client without `orchestrationProtocol: 2`. Retaining V1 therefore freezes the web client at pre-V2 too, and the store mobile app (2.0.0, protocol 2) stops connecting to a Loom server.

    **Risk:** compounding. Every provider adapter, settle/wake fix, PR watch, scheduled task and future feature is unreachable; Loom owns the pi driver alone against pi 1.x. Upstream becomes a source of ideas only.

    **Irreversible:** nothing today; the cost is the growing distance, which makes a later re-platform strictly harder than this one.

    **Loom gives up:** being a fork. This is the honest name for the option: stop syncing.
  </Column>
  <Column label="Hybrid — two engines side by side">
    **Base:** upstream for everything outside orchestration, provider and contracts; V1 kept alive beside V2 for Loom's layer while it is ported.

    **Cost:** the port plus the cost of keeping two deciders, two event stores (`orchestration_events` v1 and v2 in one file), two shell contracts and two Pi drivers compiling and consistent during the gap — and the web cannot render V1 threads under V2 contracts without a shim.

    **Risk:** every bug has two homes; the shim is precisely the dual-shape coexistence Carl's standing preferences forbid, and it tends to become permanent.

    **Verdict:** rejected as an end state or an interim. The *staging* benefit it promises — not losing Loom's features during the port — is achieved instead by keeping **production** on pre-pull-9 Loom while the integration branch is V2-only, with a feature freeze on Loom's orchestration layer until cut-over. Nothing V1 runs on the pull-9 branch at any point.
  </Column>
</Columns>

<Callout tone="decision">
**Recommendation: staged re-platform.** It is the only option under which Loom's thesis — a durable, inspectable organisation of threads the *system* keeps coherent, attributable and recoverable — keeps getting the substrate it needs from upstream (adapters, restart reconciliation, settle/wake, a tool bridge every provider shares) while Loom spends its effort on the workflow layer upstream has explicitly chosen not to build. The end state is smaller than today: the V1 engine, the V1 Pi driver, the REST transport, the goal aggregate, the launch workarounds and several columns go, and what remains sits on seams upstream has now documented as the sanctioned way for a fork to extend V2 (a closed union extended beside it; a separate migration ledger). Correctness over convenience says: pay the port once, cleanly, rather than carry two engines or stop syncing.
</Callout>

### Pull 8 (PR #323, unreviewed)

Pull 8 is upstream up to `024d49520e` — the commit before V2 — merged onto Loom, and it is exactly the merge base the trial merge used. Its 12 resolved conflicts are the pre-V2 drift; folding it into pull 9 re-does that work inside a much larger conflict set, and abandoning it throws it away while making the pull-9 textual set larger. **Land it first**, after a review scoped to "pre-V2 drift, no orchestration shape change" (which `02-loom-inventory.md` §0 premise 7 already confirms), then branch pull 9 from it. The trial merge's `rerere` preimages exist in the shared cache with no postimages, so they will not auto-resolve anything; the pull-7 tooling (`hunks.sh`, `sideresolve.py`, `union.py`, `parsesweep.mjs`, `lostdecls.py`, `aliascheck.py`) is the method.

### Phase 0 — land pull 8

Review PR #323 as pre-V2 drift and merge it via the ship procedure. Freeze Loom orchestration feature work. **Gate:** `vp check`, `vp run typecheck`, and a Pi workstream smoke on the current V1 engine so the baseline behaviour is recorded before anything moves.

### Phase 1 — mechanical merge, upstream wins on structure

Merge `upstream/main` with `merge.renameLimit=30000`. Resolve the 155 textual conflicts with the pull-7 tooling, choosing the V2 world wherever a file is where upstream wired V2 in (`ws.ts`, `server.ts`, `serverRuntimeStartup.ts`, `client-runtime/src/state/*`, `ChatView.tsx`). Take upstream's deletion on all 95 modify/delete files. Move the 86 relocated Loom files **out** of `orchestration-v2/` into a tsconfig-excluded quarantine directory so they are diffable during the port and deleted in phase 4 — never compiled. Resolve the `PiDriver.ts` add/add in upstream's favour (Loom's goes to quarantine). Adjudicate the 8 auto-merged files that lost an exported name (`McpSessionRegistry.ts`, `modelSelection.ts`, `queries.ts`, `providerIconUtils.ts`, …). Exclude Loom web modules that read `LoomThreadShellFields` from the build until phase 3d — excluded, not stubbed. **Gate:** `vp run typecheck` green on the non-quarantined tree; `vp check`; boot against a `VACUUM INTO` copy of `~/.t3/userdata/state.sqlite` and confirm `statev2.sqlite` is created from it; a vanilla Pi V2 chat turn, resume after server restart, rollback. **Dangerous:** `config.ts` has already switched `dbPath` to `statev2.sqlite` — never boot this branch against the live install.

### Phase 2 — substrate

`orchestrationV2.loom.ts` (Loom fields on `AppThread` and `ThreadShell`, commands, events, enums); the guard arm in `Orchestrator.ts` and `Orchestrator.loom.ts`; the hunk cluster in `message.dispatch` (turn-start rules, supersede, `start_if_idle`), `run.interrupt`, archive/unarchive/delete cascades, `thread.auto-settle` blockers, metadata rename; receipt-on-zero-events if V2 lacks it; Loom migrations creating the `loom_*` sidecar tables; the Loom projector and shell-query join. Pi V2 hunks: bundled pi resolution, `--session-id` first launch, open-session input fields → argv, patch 0001 extended to `switch_session`, pi bumped to 1.0.2 with the patch bundle regenerated, `pi update --self` disabled. **Gate:** typecheck; contract tests for the Loom unions decode-defaulting on upstream payloads; the ported `PiCwdOverride` contract test passing through RPC `switch_session` against the real patched pi; upstream's Pi replay fixtures still green with Loom's hunks in place. **Dangerous:** patch regeneration against the minified bundle (`patch-bundle.mjs`); the identity re-pointing — amnesia is silent, so the contract test is the gate, not a review.

### Phase 3 — control plane, tools, driver, web (four parallel tracks)

**3a** Loom MCP toolkit and handlers; `orchestration` capability withheld for Loom sessions; Loom's extension (profile fetch, `enable_toolset`, prompt debug, search guard); `ask_user_question` on V2 runtime requests. **3b** Dispatcher, fan-in, provisioner (via `defer_start` worktree strategy), liveness sweep with heartbeat from the V2 stream, exhaustion resume, handoff drafter, reaper — re-seamed on `OrchestratorV2`. **3c** Failover, retry tier, cost attribution, quotas, sanitiser re-anchored on `agent_settled`. **3d** Web surfaces re-hung on the V2 shell; `ControlDigestCard` on `notification`; goal shell-stream items. **Gate — the real Pi workstream smoke test**, run on a copied database with the dev-verify recipe: an orchestrator scaffolds a coder with an isolated worktree and a gated reviewer attached to it; the coder submits, the reviewer returns `needs_rework`, the loop runs to `clean` without waking the orchestrator; fan-in merges into the parent tree; the parent is woken once with a digest naming the report path; a second child raises `needs_guidance` and its dependent does not start; the server is restarted mid-run and the child resumes; a child with a frozen heartbeat trips the stall nudge; a `consult_thread` against a child whose worktree has been reaped answers. Plus `vp check` and `vp run typecheck`.

### Phase 4 — data import, deletions, cut-over

Loom's one-shot importer runs after upstream's legacy importer on a `VACUUM INTO` copy of production and writes `loom_*` rows for the agreed scope; the board shows the migrated goals and active workstreams. Delete the quarantine directory, Loom's V1 driver, the REST routes, the obsolete columns and migrations' dead readers; update the about 50 `state.sqlite` references; run the unmarked-hunk sweep. **Gate:** `vp check`, `vp run typecheck`, the smoke test again on the migrated copy, `pnpm ship`. (2) Session identity: a wrong lookup creates an empty same-named session and the thread forgets everything, with no error. (3) The pi bump: a regenerated patch that applies to `dist/` but not the minified bundle passes typecheck and fails at runtime. (4) `Orchestrator.ts` hunks: the next upstream pull will conflict here every time; keep to the inventory and mark every one. (5) `rerere`: the trial's preimages are in the shared cache without postimages, so nothing auto-resolves — do not expect it to. (6) The 117 silently auto-merged files, eight of which lost an exported name; `lostdecls.py` is the check. (7) A receipted deferral: any `start_if_idle` path that writes a receipt on the busy outcome never wakes that parent again, and the failure looks like a quiet orchestrator — the phase-2 deferral test and the busy-parent smoke case exist for this. (8) Imported threads without a session binding start fresh pi sessions and answer confidently from a 32,000-character summary; only the phase-4 remember-check catches it. (9) A second cut-over after a rollback silently resumes from the first snapshot.

## Round 1 rework — `plans/upstream-pull9-strategy/plan.mdx`

Commit `d420514a8e` on `t3code/plan-next-upstream-merge` (render gate clean; 12 cards/review choices, 3 tables, 10-question form). I verified every must-fix against `upstream/main` = `7812230572` before acting (`Orchestrator.ts:9713/9762/9770` for receipted rejection and zero-event rejection; `:9878–9894` per-thread lock; `:6976` respond → queued message; `:7062` dismiss refusal; `ProviderRuntimeRecoveryService.ts:289` `queueHeld`; `settings.ts:1159` continuation opt-in; `ThreadLaunchService.ts:647/892` private `schedulePreparation`; `McpHttpServer.ts` unconditional toolkit registration). All five hold. The overall recommendation is unchanged; several area cost classes, the deletion list and the mechanism for cross-thread writes are not.

### Must-fix — all accepted and implemented

**M1 (deferral + receipts).** Accepted. Area C now states that `start_if_idle` must defer *without any receipt* via a distinguished deferred error passed through `dispatchWithReceiptEffect` without `commitRejectedCommand`, and that zero-event acceptance for Loom command types is a **certain** second hunk (Loom's unchanged-value guards would otherwise become rejected tool calls). Both are described as dispatch/receipt-core hunks, not a twenty-line case. Added a phase-2 deferral test and zero-event test, a busy-parent-woken-exactly-once case to the phase-3 smoke (the case the reviewer noted the original smoke would miss), and risk item (7). Collisions table row rewritten.

**M2 (per-thread locking).** Accepted. New bullet in Area A names the concurrency-model change and commits to a mechanism: the arm writes only to the commanded thread (and threads it creates in the same command), recording decisions as Loom events (`route-taken`, `cascade-requested`); the dispatcher re-drives one idempotent per-thread command per affected thread under its own lock. Atomicity → one-pass eventual consistency, which the idempotent rails already tolerate. Ordered multi-lock rejected with the reason (non-reentrant, no deadlock guarantee). Arm relabelled **redesign** in the file tree, Area A, Area D ("port for routing, redesign for the write path"), and a new "Concurrency model" collisions row. Area D's reopen is now "disappears as a hunk but not as a step", with the gate-hold window explained.

**M3 (session identity on import).** Accepted. Area K's dangerous step is now three parts; part 1 requires the Loom importer to bind every imported thread with a pi session on disk via `thread.create.importedNativeThread{ref:{driver,nativeId,strength:"strong"}}`; the phase-4 gate continues an imported orchestrator and child and checks each remembers; the import-scope question's subtitle says the binding is not optional regardless of scope; risk item (8) added.

**M4 (Area I mechanism).** Accepted; cost class changed to **redesign**. Mechanism chosen: a Loom `runtime-request.create` command in the arm (no V2 command creates a request) plus a hunk in `runtime-request.respond` that, for a Loom-marked request with a live tool waiter, hands the answer to the waiter and emits no message; with no live waiter it falls through to V2's queued-message delivery. The settlement deletion is now conditional on that hunk existing (the fall-through is what the 343-line module approximated on V1). Dismiss stays V2's because Loom requests are `message`-capability. `ask_user_question` also moves out of the MCP toolkit into Loom's own extension (N8 — hours-long long-poll needs the reconnect loop).

**M5 (deletion list).** Accepted item by item. Notify defer queue: **kept** (queued runs are `queueHeld` on recovery and after failed runs; terminal-target check must run at delivery) — the rail delivers with `start_if_idle`. Pending-steer stash: **kept**; new Area C bullet places Loom's 28 restart-recovery hunks as a policy module on `ProviderRuntimeRecoveryService`/`RestartContinuation` and defaults `continueThreadsAfterServerUpdate` on. `origin`/`controlPayload`: **kept** as Loom message fields (shapes differ; `createdBy` has no slot); `notification` set alongside for source/summary only. Worktree provisioning: **`WorktreeProvisioner` keeps its call site** (`defer_start` only parks a run in `preparing`; preparation is reachable only via `launch`/`retryPreparation`); the "shrinks" claim removed. Stuck-launch/turn-start.fail: "verify, then delete" now names the two failure modes to reproduce under V2 and notes no V2 watchdog exists and that a wedged `starting` run would count as busy under `start_if_idle`. Area F's "four deletions" removed; the mechanism callout's "end state is smaller" is replaced with an honest Loom-side accounting (N11).

### Nice-to-have — adjudication

Implemented: **N1** (Area B now says `tools/list` is not capability-filtered; two-halves resolution — capability makes calls fail, `setActiveTools` profile keeps tools out of the prompt, ordering after the bridge's `session_start` to verify in 3a). **N2** (lane question default flipped to "keep for pull 9, collapse in a follow-up", with the storage shape settled now; the overclaim about removing reopen corrected). **N3** (sidecar record chosen explicitly; `AppThread` spread hazard cited with `7812230572`; file tree fixed). **N4** (four lineage side effects listed with accept/hunk per item). **N5** (new "Hunk inventory" table of 21 rows replacing "about six"; re-merge at every phase boundary added to the phase sketch; snapshot pinned to `a1d9d72aef` with drift noted). **N6** (re-cut-over trap in Area K and phase 4 and risk item 9). **N7** (receipts: suppress not seed — imported threads carry no Loom events, importer stamps terminal children notified; phase-4 gate checks no stale digests). **N8** (as above). **N9** (`--session-id` keeps only the *initial* name; addendum text to point at `$PI_SESSION_FILE` alone). **N10** (pull 8 misattribution corrected). **N11** (as above). **N12** (goal broadcasts outside the sequence: reconnect refetch via Loom's connect-gap subscriptions, stated in Area E). **N13** (unsolicited-guard question broadened to any delivery into pi without a server turn).

Rejected: none. Contested: none.

### One thing for the reviewer to weigh on re-verification

M2's chosen mechanism (eventual consistency via dispatcher re-drive) is a real behavioural change Carl will see on the board for one pass; the alternative the reviewer offered (a workstream-root lock taken before thread locks) was rejected because upstream's keyed executor gives no deadlock guarantee and Loom would be its only multi-key caller. If the reviewer thinks the root lock is safe given `37de6cbde6`'s shared keyed lock, that is worth saying — it would make Area D's reopen atomic again.

<addendum>
You operate inside T3 Code's work model: Goals → Tasks → Workstream. This is how every thread here is organised, whatever its role.

A GOAL is a single durable objective that outlives any one session and spans many — the north star for all work under it. Orient to it; if work drifts from the goal, refocus or update it. A goal is decomposed into a TASK TREE: the living, shared record of what is done and what remains — for the agents working it and for the human who glances at it to re-orient. It is kept current as work progresses.

Work happens in a WORKSTREAM: a tree of durable threads. You are one thread in it, and your role overlay says how you act within it. A ROOT thread ORCHESTRATES — it plans, delegates, and reviews rather than doing the work by hand. A CHILD thread EXECUTES a single self-contained brief and hands a result back. A child is a real, persistent thread a human can open and talk to, not a throwaway: spawning one is deliberate, and a child starts fresh — it inherits none of the parent's conversation, only the brief it is given. Work flows down as briefs and back up as reports. The workstream is a graph of threads: dependencies are its edges, so dependent work waits while independent branches run in parallel (with bounded review-gate loops as the one deliberate cycle) — and the graph is not fixed; it is expected to be amended and replanned as understanding improves.

Getting information from another thread, cheapest first: a thread's REPORT is its curated hand-back — read that first. The workstream GRAPH lets you see every thread and find any of them without searching (`workstream_list`). To resolve an ambiguity, CONSULT the thread that holds the context. The full thread history can be accessed via the Pi session jsonl file if necessary.

A few principles keep this coherent:
- Your assignment is your task. For a child that is its spawn brief; at the root it is the user's direction. An inherited goal is background - align to it, but where it and your assignment differ, follow the assignment.
- Work at your level, and keep heavy sub-phases out of your context. If you orchestrate, delegate substantial work to children rather than absorbing it inline, and when new non-trivial work crystallises mid-conversation, pause to lay out or amend the graph before diving in. If you execute a brief, do it yourself rather than re-delegating it — but any thread, at any depth, may hand a bounded sub-phase of its own brief to a child when all three hold: the sub-phase is context-heavy; a short brief can carry everything it needs from you; and what comes back is an artefact — files on disk plus a short report — not understanding you must carry into later turns. Typical cases: a screenshot-capture pass, a large-corpus read, a bulk extraction. Done in situ, every page of that stays in your context for the rest of the thread; done by a child, it dies with the child. It is a trade, not a reflex: a child starts cold, so you pay to write the brief and to wait for it — a sub-phase of a few turns is cheaper inline. Where the delegation tools are dormant for your role, `enable_toolset` activates them.
- Status describes the plan; runtime is the truth. A thread's status is where it sits in the workflow; whether its agent is actually working is a separate, system-tracked fact. Lean on the system's signals for a child's state rather than inferring from a single quiet look — and if a signal looks wrong for what you can plainly see, verify rather than act blindly.
- System notices are not the human. Automated workstream notices (a child finished, needs attention, recovered) are control-plane signals for you to act on, not messages from the user.
- Your worktree is your workspace. Every edit and commit you make lands in your own worktree (your process cwd) and nowhere else — any other checkout of this project (another thread's worktree, the parent's worktree, or the project's base workspace root) is read-only context (reports, evidence), never somewhere to `cd` into and write. This matters doubly if you orchestrate: children's worktrees are cut from YOUR branch, so a file committed anywhere else — however canonical its path looks — is invisible to every child you spawn. If a brief seems to require editing outside your own worktree, that is a brief error: surface it rather than comply.
- File references in replies and reports: use the full absolute path in inline code, one span per file or directory. Do not use bare basenames, paths relative to a shell `cd`, or fenced blocks for these references. The client resolves relative paths from the thread's worktree root, not the cwd inside a bash command.
- Search your worktree, not the roots above it. Your worktree is small, but the workspace and cockpit roots that contain it are vast (every sibling worktree's node_modules), so an unbounded `find`/`grep` from one of those roots can crawl for many minutes. Never search them unscoped: stay within your worktree, or bound the walk (`-maxdepth`, a named subtree, or a tool like `rg` that skips gitignored trees) rather than let a search wander into other threads' trees. A guard blocks unbounded recursive searches outside your worktree and auto-bounds unbounded search pipelines to 30s — when a file is not where you expected, do not search wider: verify the exact paths your brief gave you first (brief paths are authoritative), then run a focused bounded search, and only as a last resort consult the thread that holds the context (`consult_thread` — expensive).
- Setup may still be running. Worktree environment setup can run in the background after you start, so before any command that needs the project environment (installs, builds, tests, typecheck, dev servers) check the setup breadcrumb — `cat "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/t3code-setup-state.json"`: `ready` proceed; `pending` do reading/editing/planning first and re-check (poll, don't run installs yourself); `failed` inspect its `detail` and the setup terminal output, then fix or report the setup failure rather than blindly rerunning installs; file absent means no setup script was configured — assume the repo is in its normal provided state.

You are thread `8bbbfc3e-82d7-47a7-9de5-4760de713f28` in this workstream: the id every workstream tool takes, the id the human sees, and the id you quote when reporting. Your own conversation history is the pi session jsonl at `$PI_SESSION_FILE` (set in every shell command you run), a file named `*_8bbbfc3e-82d7-47a7-9de5-4760de713f28.jsonl`. To reach ANOTHER thread's history, use its report or `consult_thread`; its jsonl is not necessarily in the same directory as yours.

You are a planner sub-thread. Produce intent briefs and implementation plans — the thinking, not the code.

- Your spawn brief defines your assignment — the plan you owe, not a script. If you discover the brief rests on a wrong assumption, or planning surfaces something material it didn't anticipate, surface it (in the plan's risks, or via `needs_guidance` if it invalidates the brief) rather than silently re-scoping.
- Your deliverable is a plan, not an implementation. Investigate the codebase as deeply as needed, but do not write feature code — decisions and their rationale are what you hand back.
- Author plans as annotatable MDX documents per the mdx-visual-plan skill (`plans/<slug>/plan.mdx`), so the human can review and annotate them in-app before any code is written.
- A good plan states intent, decomposition into work items, contracts and risks, and acceptance criteria — enough that its correctness can be judged before implementation.
- Write for a reader with none of your context. The coder threads that implement the plan inherit nothing you've read or reasoned through; the plan must stand alone.
- Never use internal ids ('D1', 'must-fix #2') as decision titles or QuestionForm labels; name the decision and each option's outcome so they stand alone.
- Keep the task tree honest. If you are anchored, that branch is yours: tick your own tasks with `goal_task_update` the moment they land, and reshape it in ONE `goal_tasks_rewrite` if its shape stops matching the work. Tasks outside your branch are read-only — say what needs doing there in your report. Record actionable work your planning surfaces with `goal_task_add` under the phase it belongs to. Your plan's decomposition is not yours to impose on the rest of the tree: hand that intended shape back in your report, along with details, findings and verdicts.
- If your scope has sharpened beyond your spawn title, you may rename yourself with `set_thread_title` (it only ever renames the calling thread) to keep the sidebar legible.
- Your `workstream_submit` report leads with the plan's location and its key decisions. When implementation must not start until a human has approved the plan, raise `awaiting_acceptance` via `workstream_request_attention` **instead of completing** — the raise is what holds the plan, and completing in the same turn releases the coders the approval was meant to gate. Raise it only when work genuinely must wait; a plan no human has to see first just completes.

SHIPPING POLICY: merge authority is AGENT-OK — once the work is approved and required checks pass, an agent may land it on the main branch, but only by merging a PR from a feature branch via the repo's guarded ship procedure (the ship skill / `pnpm ship` where present). Never push directly to the main branch and never merge by hand; then clean up the branch.

Background context — your parent orchestrator is working toward this overall goal `ea6cb872-9915-41fc-9bed-921a93cc1d2c` (plan-next-upstream-t3-code-merge-into-loom): Pull 9 strategy: Orchestration V2 alignment
Parent's objective (background only, NOT your task): Begin working out how to proceed with the next upstream pingdotgg/t3code merge into the Loom fork, which is expected to be much more complex due to substantial upstream orchestration rewrites and new native Pi support that overlaps heavily with Loom.

What follows is a spawn snapshot of the branch you own; `goal_task_list` reads it live.

Where your branch sits in the goal (read-only context, not rewrite input):
  Decide the pull-9 strategy: adopt V2 and re-express Loom on it, retain Loom's engine, or hybrid — per area and overall (87d1bd9f-8c4f-4515-a5d9-747173128bbe)

Your branch — its root line is your anchor, and this block is the complete source a branch rewrite takes:
- [x] Synthesise the four inventories into a reviewable per-area decision document with a recommended mechanism (f8a548a1-c6d2-437a-a851-7ba8da0fc771)

Goal pulse: 7/8 done · 1 open task · 1 open outside your branch — `goal_task_list` with scope "tree" reads all of it.

Tick your own tasks with `goal_task_update` as each lands, and reshape your branch in ONE `goal_tasks_rewrite` when its shape stops matching the work: submit exactly the branch block above, keeping every retained `(id)`; your anchor stays its root line. Tasks outside your branch are read-only — record discovered work with `goal_task_add` (it lands in your branch by default; pass a parentTaskId to place it elsewhere, and the echo shows where it landed) and say what needs doing in your report. Anything you write is a short plain-language work item naming the outcome and value, for a reader outside this thread (the server rejects text over 300 characters); details, findings and verdicts go in your report or memo.

# Coding rules

## Optimise the end state, not the diff

Optimise for the best business outcome the task serves, then for the fewest lines and moving parts that deliver it at the same performance — a −2000/+200 diff that does so beats a +50 one. Scope follows that outcome, not the initial file list. Do not drop useful behaviour, or reject a necessary cross-package or cross-repo fix, merely to keep the diff small.

- Prefer comprehensions, generator expressions, and standard library utilities over verbose loops and ceremony.
- Prefer direct expressions over scaffolding variables.
- Prefer one canonical happy path; avoid "helpful" alternate paths.

## Compression Checklist (run before finalising)

After drafting a solution, do a compression pass:

- Inline single-use variables where they don't materially clarify intent.
- Replace loops with comprehensions/generators where readability allows.
- Remove helper functions used only once unless they're materially clarifying.
- Combine related conditional branches.
- Collapse single-statement if/else where a direct expression suffices.

## Tests are Optional and Rare

Do not default to adding tests. This codebase is at prototype stage and frequently refactored; tests written for code that's about to be replaced cost twice (write now, delete later) and lock in implementation details that the refactor will obsolete.

Propose tests only when change risk is genuinely high; explain why in plain language. Prefer lightweight validation on real code and real data over mock-heavy unit tests.

## Verify with the canonical entrypoint

Unit tests are necessary but insufficient. If the project documents a canonical entrypoint (e.g. a `run.py` you can invoke via `python -m`, a `main` command, a documented "recommended entrypoint" from a setup script), **invoke it at least once against real data** before declaring the task complete.

A green unit-test suite plus a passing canonical-entrypoint run is the bar for "done"; either alone is not. Synthetic in-memory smoke tests built with fabricated fixtures are weaker still — they don't catch contract drift between functions you wrote in the same session, and they don't catch real-data shape surprises.

If the canonical entrypoint requires resources you don't have access to (an API key, real input data, a deployed service), say so explicitly in your final summary instead of silently substituting a synthetic smoke test for the real verification.

## No backwards compatibility in prototypes

This codebase is a prototype. Prototypes never preserve backwards
compatibility on internal schemas, output artefacts, or pipeline
contracts. There is no production downstream to protect; the cost of
"preserved for backward compatibility" code is permanent surface area
on a contract that is supposed to be migrating freely. The whole point
of prototype velocity is the freedom to delete cleanly.

Hard rules:

- Do not add fields "kept for backward compatibility" alongside their
  replacements. Delete the old field; emit only the new one.
- Do not add sidecar files, derived-field facades, or dual-shape
  output that paper over a schema migration. If a downstream
  debugging or analysis script reads the old shape, update the script
  — do not preserve the old shape to keep the script working.
- Debugging/analysis artefacts are never load-bearing. Treating a
  debugging sidecar as a reason to keep the old wire shape on the
  production payload is insane: it inverts the dependency direction.
  The sidecar follows the schema, not the other way around.
- Do not invent a "backward compatibility" justification for keeping
  a legacy form. If the migration is too big to do cleanly, surface
  that to the user and let them decide to defer the migration
  explicitly — do not silently implement the shim and present it as
  the only option.
- When the controlling architecture / design / intent document says
  "no coexistence period", "no compat shim", "breaking change", or
  any equivalent, reviewers must reject any patch that introduces a
  shim. The phrase "for backward compatibility" appearing in a diff
  comment, docstring, schema field description, or PR description is
  a review-stopping flag unless the user has explicitly approved
  that specific shim for that specific change.

## Automated review feedback is a claim, not a verdict

When an automated reviewer (Copilot, a linter, a CI bot) flags code you wrote deliberately, do NOT default to agreeing. Before changing anything, restate *why* the code is that way and *who consumes the behaviour the suggestion would change*. A reviewer has less context than you about audience and intent — it cannot see that this is a dev-only tool, a prototype, or a deliberate omission. "I wrote/introduced this" is a reason to defend a considered choice, not to assume guilt — guilt-framing skips evaluation. Reject suggestions whose premise doesn't hold for this code's actual consumer; accept only the ones that survive that test. The specific failure this guards against: reversing a decision you made minutes ago, with sound reasoning, the instant a lower-context bot disagrees.

## Filesystem search scope

Do not run `find` rooted at `$HOME`, `~`, or `/`. Carl's home contains ~10 active fathom worktrees (each ~5000 files), `~/.cache/claude-cli-nodejs/` with dozens of session worktree-pattern dirs, `~/.roo/`, and various tool caches — unscoped finds traverse millions of files and take minutes, not seconds. Scope to the smallest plausible subtree: project root (`git rev-parse --show-toplevel`), `~/pi-craft/`, `~/pi-fathom/`, or `~/.pi/agent/{skills,agents}/`. Skills, agents, and extensions are already listed in the pi startup banner — reference that list before searching disk for them. For name-based search prefer `rg --files | rg <pattern>` over `find`; it respects `.gitignore` and is an order of magnitude faster.

## Slack goes through Carl-Roobot

Every Slack action — DM, group DM, file, channel post — uses the **Carl-Roobot bot token** in `~/.config/carl-roobot/config.json`, whose `team` map resolves first names to Slack user ids. Do NOT use `~/.slack/credentials.json` (a personal app-development OAuth token: it authenticates but `missing_scope`s on every send) and do NOT use the `slack` CLI (it builds Slack *apps*; it cannot send messages). Do not broaden the scopes on Carl's personal token — ask instead.

Three jobs, three paths; the scripts exist because each has a step that is silently wrong when hand-rolled:

- **Send a file** → `~/loom-slack-bridge/scripts/slack-attach --to <names> --file <path> --text "..."`. Attaches directly. Over ~10 MB, or when the recipient needs a revocable link, use the `share-files` skill's GCS path instead.
- **Open a conversation whose replies come back to you** → `~/loom-slack-bridge/scripts/convene --with <names> --text "..."` for a group DM, or `--channel '#name'` to post into a channel Carl-Roobot has been invited to (it cannot list channels, and gets `not_in_channel` until invited). The opening message must carry `loom_thread` metadata or replies never reach the calling thread; the script stamps it. Tell participants to *reply in-thread* — a new top-level message does not route back.
- **Notify a PR author** → the `pr-review` skill's `pr_notify_slack.sh`.

## Self-improvement: when to propose a rule

If you hit a recurring pattern that this doc doesn't address — and a rule would prevent its recurrence — propose adding one. Two paths by scope:

- **Specific or contextual** (project-specific paths, single-pattern correction, learned-from-mistake) → use `memory_remember`. Memory injects into every future session automatically; no review needed.
- **Broad or structural** (philosophy, cross-project workflow, architectural constraint) → edit `~/pi-craft/AGENTS.md` and surface the diff to the user for review. Do not auto-commit AGENTS.md changes — they affect every future session, so the user holds the merge button. Log the trigger in `~/pi-craft/docs/agents-md-history.md` when you propose.

Bias against adding rules. The pi-craft option-b ablation found that most positive-directive rules are inert on frontier models; only negative constraints and the rare specific-failure-mode rule earn their tokens. If the model already does the right thing without the rule, don't add the rule.
