# T3 Code

T3 Code is a minimal GUI for coding agents. A Node WebSocket server wraps provider CLIs and agents (Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, Antigravity) and serves web, desktop, and mobile clients.

You can think of T3 Code as an open source "bring-your-own-subscription" alternative to apps like Claude Desktop, Codex App, Cursor Glass and Conductor.

## What makes T3 Code special?

We have over 400,000 users who love T3 Code. It's important we maintain the things they love as we continue to iterate on the product. Here's a brief list of the things we can never compromise on.

### 1. Open at the core

T3 Code is truly open. We share our roadmap, we share how we think about things, and of course we share all our code. A large number of our users run forks. We work in the open, and should strive to stay that way.

### 2. Performance without compromise

Lots of apps have gotten bogged down with bad tech decisions and "slop". We have not, and we're proud of the performance of T3 Code. We regularly audit for performance regressions, often caused by sending too much data over websockets, css animations causing gpu spikes, lists being hard to render, and more. Make sure all changes are considerate of performance impact.

### 3. Remote ready

The architecture of T3 Code's websocket layer (npx t3) enables a lot of awesome remote features. These have become core to the product. Whether users are connecting directly over their local network, using Tailscale, or leaning in fully with T3 Connect (our tunnel solution, also in this repo), we need to make sure new features are properly supported.

### 4. Multi-surface

T3 Code has 3 key app surfaces: **web**, **desktop**, and **mobile**.

**Web** is kind of two surfaces, as we have the public facing "app.t3.codes" as well as locally hosting the web app through the `npx t3` command. Both need to be supported by all new features where reasonable.

**Desktop** is the main surface most users install first. It's a full Electron app that bundles the server runner as well. The desktop app can also be used as the host server, allowing remote connections from app.t3.codes or the mobile app.

**Mobile** is a React Native app for both iOS and Android, available on the App Store and Google Play. The mobile app allows for connecting to any T3 Code server to control work remotely.

## A note from Theo

I like ambitious ideas, simple systems, and software that feels obvious. Do not preserve complexity just because it already exists. Do not introduce machinery because it looks architecturally impressive. Understand the real constraint, then fight for the smallest model that makes the correct behavior unsurprising.

Channel both "measure twice, cut once" and "yagni". Fight scope creep. Try to honor the dev's intent in both a minimal and realistic fashion.

The rest of this document is meant to help you navigate the codebase and make changes effectively. Think of these instructions less as "hard rules", more as "good defaults". The developer's preferences should be able to override anything here.

Of note: Most T3 Code contributions will come from T3 Code itself, often controlled remotely. This means you should be careful about accessing data, killing dev servers, and other things that may damage the T3 Code instance that the contributor is using.

## A small glossary

We need to be on the same page with terminology. When communicating, use this language:

- **you** means the agent reading this file and changing T3 Code.
- **we, us, and maintainers** mean Theo, Julius and the people building T3 Code. These are who you are talking to now.
- **user** means the person using T3 Code to direct coding agents.
- **agent** means the coding agent a user runs inside T3 Code. Depending on context, that may also include you.
- **provider** means the agent runtime or harness T3 Code talks to, such as Codex, Claude, Cursor, or OpenCode.
- **client** means the web, desktop, or mobile UI.
- **environment** means one running T3 server and the machine, filesystem, provider credentials, and state it owns.
- **project** means an environment-local workspace record rooted at a directory.
- **thread** means the durable conversation and work history for a project.
- **turn** means one user-to-agent cycle, including follow-up work such as checkpointing.
- **T3 home** means the base data directory. Runtime state normally lives below its userdata directory.

## Task Completion Requirements (loom)

- `vp check` and `vp run typecheck` must pass before considering tasks completed.
  - If changing native mobile code, `vp run lint:mobile` must also pass.
- Use `vp test` for the built-in Vite+ test command and `vp run test` when you specifically need the `test` package script.

> This supersedes upstream's "Do not run repo-wide checks" bullet under
> [Verifying](#verifying): loom has no CI that owns the full suite, so the gates
> run locally before anything is called done.

## Shipping changes (commit, PR, merge)

The canonical procedure (branch → commit → rebase → PR → merge → cleanup, plus
this repo's fork/worktree gotchas) lives in
[`docs/operations/shipping.md`](docs/operations/shipping.md) — the single source
of truth. Run the mechanical sequence with `pnpm ship -m "<summary>"` (it is
encoded in `scripts/ship.ts`); the `ship` skill loads the procedure inline and
the `shipper` role is the delegated path. In a workstream, spawn a `shipper`
child once the work is approved or ship inline via the `ship` skill; outside a
workstream, follow the doc directly. Do not ship until the user has approved
shipping the change.

**Merge authority is per-project**, declared in `.t3code/ship.json` (resolved by
walking up from the working directory) and injected into every thread's system
prompt as the SHIPPING POLICY block. The platform default is `human` — agents
open the PR and stop for a human to review and merge; **loom itself is `agent`**,
so the flow above carries through the merge. Never merge under a `human` policy,
even when a brief's definition of done says "merged". See
[`docs/operations/shipping.md`](docs/operations/shipping.md) for the policy shape
and rationale.

Shipping ends at the merge. **Deploying to the production VM is a separate,
human-initiated act** — never deploy as part of finishing a change unless the
user explicitly asks for a deploy. When asked, the mechanism lives in
`~/loom-releases/RUNBOOK.md` (loom-slack-bridge repo); never run a raw in-place
`pnpm cockpit:build`.

This supersedes upstream's "Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks"
bullet only in the sense that the approval gate is the user's _shipping_ approval;
the PR itself is still never opened unprompted.

## Database migrations

Migrations run in two independent ledgers. Loom migrations are **numbered `1001+`**
and registered in `apps/server/src/persistence/LoomMigrations.ts`; upstream's
`Migrations.ts` is kept byte-identical to upstream, so never edit it and never
number a fork migration below `1000` (doing so silently disables future upstream
migrations on existing databases). Rationale and the reconciliation design are in
[`docs/upstream-sync/22-migration-lane-split-plan.md`](docs/upstream-sync/22-migration-lane-split-plan.md).

## Loom UI state conventions

Loom UI state belongs to one of four tiers, and automatic surface openers must _seed_ state without ever _overriding_ a user's persisted choice. Before adding client UI state, classify it against [`docs/architecture/loom-ui-state-tiers.md`](docs/architecture/loom-ui-state-tiers.md) (tier table, seed-not-override write policy, the retained plan-auto-open exception, and the orphan-key note).

## Live frontend verification

UI-affecting changes should be verified live in the browser, not just by static checks. Two paths:

- **Full app — dev-verify recipe** ([`docs/dev-site-testing.md`](docs/dev-site-testing.md)): stands up an isolated dev instance, seeds a realistic workstream (`apps/server/src/dev/seedWorkstream.ts`), reads the pairing URL from stdout, and drives the authenticated app in the browser. Briefs can just say "verify live using the dev-verify recipe". Use this for flows that need real threads, auth, or server state.
- **Isolated component — preview harness** ([`docs/web-component-preview.md`](docs/web-component-preview.md)): a dev-only `/preview` route (no backend) that renders presentational components (`ChatMarkdown`, tables, code blocks, …) against fixtures reproducing the real timeline layout chain. Use this for pure render/CSS work — it's a ~seconds loop. Add a fixture in `apps/web/src/preview/fixtures.tsx` for the case you're changing.

## HTML artefacts (mockups, visual reports, explainers)

Standalone HTML produced for a human to view — a mockup, a visual report, an
explainer — goes in the gitignored `.artifacts/` directory at the worktree
root: write it with the ordinary file-write tool and cite the
workspace-relative path (e.g. `.artifacts/quota-mockup.html`) in chat, which
renders it in-app via the file chip's View affordance. Relative subresources
resolve, so a multi-file artefact works — keep all its files under one
subdirectory of `.artifacts/`. Pick a fresh descriptive filename and never
overwrite an existing artefact — the worktree may be shared with other
threads, and a chat chip renders whatever is on disk now. Do not write
renderable HTML to locations outside the worktree (the `visual_explainer`
tool's `~/.agent/diagrams/` default cannot be rendered in-app — write the
HTML to `.artifacts/` instead), and do not commit throwaway HTML under
`experiments/` or `docs/`. For a reviewable plan or recap, prefer the MDX
genres (`plans/<slug>/plan.mdx`, `recaps/<slug>/recap.mdx`) over a standalone
HTML artefact.

## Fork-specific notes

- Loom is a **Pi-first fork**: `PI_DEFAULT_MODEL` is the default model and the
  driver registry deliberately ships pi only. Upstream's multi-provider
  guidance ("Providers: Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, and OpenCode each have an
  adapter") applies to the adapters that remain, not to the registry.
- Upstream sync doctrine and per-area resolutions live in
  [`docs/upstream-sync/`](docs/upstream-sync/).
- **Mark every loom hunk.** Any hunk you add to a file that also exists
  upstream carries a `// loom:` comment; larger additions belong in a
  `*.loom.ts` module or `apps/web/src/loom/`. Unmarked hunks are invisible to
  the lost-feature audit and are silently dropped at the next upstream pull.
  The `pnpm ship` gate enforces this
  (`docs/upstream-sync/pull7-tools/unmarkedsweep.sh`); the convention is in
  [`docs/upstream-sync/23-sidebar-v2-rehome.md`](docs/upstream-sync/23-sidebar-v2-rehome.md).
- **Never `git stash` in this repo.** Every worktree shares one `.git`, so the
  stash stack is global across all concurrent threads and a `pop` can hand you
  another thread's work and drop yours. Commit a WIP (`--no-verify`) or use
  `git diff > patch` / `git apply` instead.

## The three ways to hurt yourself

1. **Killing by pattern.** Never `pkill -f`, `pgrep | kill`, or `kill` a PID you found by matching a name, path, or worktree string. Your own agent process has this worktree's path in its argv, and this machine runs several other dev servers at once. Kill only a PID you captured at spawn, or the owner of your port from `ss -H -ltnp` after confirming `/proc/<pid>/cwd` is your worktree.
2. **Writing to the live install.** `~/.t3/userdata` is the developer's real T3 Code database, in use while you work. Reading it and copying from it are fine, and a good way to get real test data (see Test data). Never start a server against it, never open it read-write, never clean it up.
3. **Baking in origins.** Never set `VITE_HTTP_URL` or `VITE_WS_URL` for dev. Dev is single-origin and Vite proxies `/api`, `/ws`, `/oauth`, and `/.well-known`. Setting them bakes localhost into the bundle and silently breaks every remote browser.

## Hit every surface

The most common defect in this repo is a change that works on the path you tested and is missing everywhere else. Before calling frontend work done, walk this list and say which entries applied:

- **Entry points.** A behavior reachable from the chat view is usually also reachable from Settings, the command palette, and a keybinding. Fixing one is not fixing the feature.
- **Clients.** Web, desktop (wraps web, adds Electron shell/IPC), and mobile (React Native, separate navigation). Shared logic lives in `packages/client-runtime`
- **Providers.** Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok, OpenCode, and Antigravity each have an adapter. Provider-shaped features need a decision per adapter, even if the decision is "not supported here".
- **Agents.** A capability a user can trigger is usually one an agent should reach through MCP tools, and scheduled tasks run the same paths. That only works when it is a service method, not handler code.
- **Contracts.** Anything crossing the wire is typed in `packages/contracts`. Change the schema and the server, web, mobile, and desktop all follow.
- **Reverse states.** If you added a way in, add the way out and the way to see it. Snooze needs unsnooze. Close needs reopen. A one-way door is a bug.
- **Connection modes.** Local, remote/relay, and tunnel behave differently. Multi-device and multi-environment cases are real.
- **Docs.** Check whether the change makes existing guidance inaccurate. Apply the [documentation rules](#documentation) before adding anything.

## Dev servers

- `vp i` installs. Worktrees get this from the t3.json setup script; if module resolution looks broken, it probably did not run.
- `vp run dev` starts server and web. In a worktree, state defaults to that worktree's gitignored `.t3`, which deliberately outranks an ambient `T3CODE_HOME` so you cannot land on shared state by accident. An explicit `--home-dir` still wins. The server enforces the same default: a checkout provisioned under `<home>/worktrees/` runs on its own `.t3` even when booted by hand as `node apps/server/src/bin.ts serve`, and one INFO line at startup names the rule that chose the home. Passing `--base-dir "$PWD/.t3"` still says it explicitly, and remains the habit worth keeping. A boot also refuses outright when another live server already holds that home's `state.sqlite`; clear it by deleting `<stateDir>/server-runtime.json` only when you know that pid is not a server.
- Ports derive from the worktree path and are stable across restarts, but read the real ones from the `[dev-runner]` line since occupied ports shift.
- Sharing over the tailnet is three steps: run `vp run dev --share` in the background, wait for the `pairingUrl:` line in its output, then give that full URL to an unpaired browser. Do not wire up `tailscale serve` by hand, open the URL yourself, or consume the user's pairing link. A browser with the reusable dev cookie can use the bare origin. If a normal one-time token was consumed, mint a fresh one with `node apps/server/src/bin.ts pair`. It carries standard scopes, while the startup URL carries admin scopes needed for Connections settings.
- To reuse web dev auth across worktrees, configure one fixed `T3CODE_DEV_AUTH_TOKEN` in the main checkout's gitignored `.env`. The `t3.json` setup links that file into worktrees. Never commit or publish the token or a startup URL. See [Reusable dev credential](docs/operations/development.md#reusable-dev-credential).
- Stop what you started, by the PID you tracked. See rule 1.

## Test data

An empty database is a bad test. Seed your worktree's `.t3` with a copy of real data instead of pointing at live state:

- Copy from `~/.t3/userdata` (the developer's real data, the most realistic test set) or `~/.t3/dev`. Worktree state lives at `<worktree>/.t3/userdata`.
- Snapshot the database with `VACUUM INTO`, which is safe even while a server has the source open and yields one consistent file:

  ```bash
  mkdir -p .t3/userdata
  rm -f .t3/userdata/state.sqlite*  # VACUUM INTO refuses to overwrite
  bun -e "new (require('bun:sqlite').Database)(process.env.HOME + '/.t3/userdata/state.sqlite', { readonly: true }).run(\"VACUUM INTO '.t3/userdata/state.sqlite'\")"
  ```

  A plain `cp` is only safe when no server has the source open, and must bring the `-wal` and `-shm` siblings along. A live file copy is a corrupt copy.

- Bring `secrets` and `settings.json` only if the flow under test needs them.
- Copy in, never symlink. Data flows one way: into your sandbox, never back out.

## Verifying

- Smallest proof that the change works. `vp test run <files>` for the tests you touched, targeted lint and typecheck for the scope you changed.
- Test meaningful logic or observable behavior. Do not render components to static markup to assert props or attributes, or add tests that merely assert callback wiring or mirror the implementation.
- **Do not run repo-wide checks.** No `vp check`, no `vp run -r test`, no `vp run -r typecheck` unless I ask. CI owns the full suite.
- Backend behavior changes ship with focused tests for that behavior.
- The server is event-sourced and its async flows emit typed receipts. Wait on receipts and worker drains, never on sleeps or polling. A test that needs a timeout to pass is wrong.
- Upon request, user-visible frontend changes should get one integrated pass in a real client: `test-t3-app` for web, `test-t3-mobile` for mobile. The primary agent does this once after integrating. Subagents do not launch their own dev servers. Ask permission before doing computer use or spinning up browsers.

For authorized mobile verification, a missing or outdated native client is a build step, not a blocker. Run `node scripts/mobile-native-client.ts ensure <ios|android> <device-id>` on the simulator host before starting Metro. It checks the local Expo fingerprint and builds/installs when needed. See `test-t3-mobile` for the full workflow.

## Pull requests

- Never make a PR unless the developer explicitly asks you to do so.
- Conventional commit titles, plain language: `fix(web): new threads no longer spike CPU`.
- Body: the problem in a sentence or two, then how you fixed it. End with the model and harness that did the work.
- UI changes need before/after images. Motion or timing needs a short video.
- Upload PR evidence to GitHub. Never commit PR-only screenshots or assets such as `.github/pr-assets/`.
- One concern per PR. If the description says "also", split it.
- When babysitting: poll checks and comments newer than the last push, verify each bot finding against the source, fix real ones, dismiss false positives with a written reason. Stay quiet when nothing is new. Stop when the bots are green on the latest commit.

## Documentation

Most code changes do not need an internal documentation change. Agents can read the code.

- `docs/internals/` is for architectural decisions and their reasons, constraints that span components, and implementation traps that are hard to discover from the source. Before adding a paragraph, ask what a maintainer would get wrong without it. If reading the relevant code answers the question, leave it out.
- Do not document every feature, enumerate fields or methods, narrate control flow, maintain file catalogs, or append PR summaries. Types, tests, and code already record the implementation. The glossary defines shared vocabulary; it is not a feature index.
- Keep a local implementation explanation in a nearby code comment. Use an internal doc when the reasoning crosses boundaries or needs context the code cannot carry well. Link to the relevant source instead of copying it.
- When a documented decision or constraint changes, rewrite or remove the affected text. Do not append another account of the new behavior. A new internal page needs a distinct, durable reason to exist.
- `docs/user/` helps users accomplish tasks. Give each major feature a concise section explaining what it does, how to start, and anything unintuitive. A settings path is useful; descriptions of visible buttons, icons, layouts, animations, or every UI state are not. Before adding text, ask what task or decision it helps the user with.
- Keep user docs in the shipped product's voice, without implementation details or contributor tooling. Update the relevant feature section when how to use it changes. A UI tweak does not need a documentation entry, and a new control does not need its own page.
- `docs/operations/` holds maintainer setup, release, and debugging procedures. Keep instructions for operating an installed T3 Code server in the user guides.

## Plans and work artifacts

- Do not commit implementation plans, research notes, or agent scratch files. Keep temporary working material outside the worktree. `.plans/` is gitignored only as a safety net for legacy tooling.
- Track active maintainer work in the GitHub issue or project item that owns it. External proposals follow `CONTRIBUTING.md` and belong in Ideas discussions.
- A merged PR is the implementation record. Close or update its tracking item when the work lands; do not preserve a second checklist in the repository.

## How it works

Clients send typed WebSocket requests. The server turns them into _commands_, a pure _decider_ turns commands into persisted _events_, and a _projector_ derives the read model the UI renders. Provider CLIs run as subprocesses; per-provider _adapters_ translate their native protocols into orchestration events. Side effects run in queue-backed _reactors_ that emit _receipts_ when milestones land. Each turn ends with a _checkpoint_, a hidden git ref, so the app can diff and restore.

Full glossary with file links: `docs/internals/glossary.md`

## Where code lives

- `apps/server` - WebSocket, orchestration, providers, checkpointing. Effect-heavy: read [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md) before adding server code, and `.repos/effect-smol/LLMS.md` for the Effect library itself.
- `apps/web` - React/Vite UI. `apps/desktop` wraps it, `apps/mobile` is React Native, `apps/marketing` is the site.
- `packages/contracts` - Effect/Schema contracts plus small derived helpers. No heavy runtime logic.
- `packages/shared` - shared runtime utils, subpath exports, no barrel.
- `packages/client-runtime` - client code shared by web and mobile.
- `.repos/` - vendored read-only references. Prefer their patterns over invented ones. Never edit or import from them. Sync with `vpr sync:repos` when bumping the matching dependency.

## Taste

- Complexity belongs at the adapter boundary. Orchestration stays pure, UI stays dumb.
- Server features are services; transports stay thin. A `ws.ts` RPC handler, HTTP route, or MCP tool decodes input, calls one service method, and maps errors. See [Effect services](docs/internals/effect-services.md).
- `apps/web/src/components/ui` exports own their look. Pick a `variant` or `size`; do not restyle one with `className`. If none fits and the look is a generic concept, add a variant to the component; a look that belongs to one feature stays in that feature's own component, not in `components/ui`. Layout classes (width, flex, margin, position) belong on the parent. `shadcn/no-restyle` fails lint on violations.
- Inferred types over annotations. `any` is the enemy.
- Comments describe how a thing is used, and move when the code moves. To be used mostly to describe functions, not to annotate every line of behavior.
- Our users drive agents all day and notice a dropped frame, a lying spinner, and a stale label. No continuously repainting animations; they peg the GPU on high-refresh displays.
- If a rule here fights the task in front of you, say so loudly and get a human sign-off before breaking it.

## Additional tips

- Don't verify with browsers or computer use unless the user explicitly agrees or requests it.
- Security is important, but should not be over-indexed on, especially for dev mode/maintainer-only features.

</project_instructions>
</project_context>

# Revision 2 of `plans/upstream-pull9-strategy/plan.mdx` — Carl has answered, and the ground has moved

Carl reviewed the document in-app and recorded his decisions. Three things changed that the plan must absorb, plus two annotations to answer in the text. The branch has moved: I merged `origin/main` into `t3code/plan-next-upstream-merge` (now `d4941a13dc`) and **renumbered the four reports to `docs/upstream-sync/28-pull9-v2-alignment/`** (27 was already pull 8's set); the plan's references are updated. Work from the current tree.

## 1. Pull 8 is merged and in production — and it changed after we analysed it

PR #323 merged on 2026-10-05 10:41Z, and `origin/main` `8368a63b16` is deployed. Q2 ("what happens to pull 8") is therefore answered by events: **Phase 0 is done**; delete the question and rewrite Phase 0 / the "Pull 8" subsection / the five-facts item as a statement. The merge-base with `upstream/main` is unchanged (`024d49520e`), so the trial-merge counts stand in shape; say the base moved and that the counts were measured against the PR tip.

More important: three follow-on PRs landed that our four reports never saw, and Carl's words were *"make sure that you review the changes that were made to pull 8"*:
- **#325 "pull 8 review reversals — Carl's Tier A rulings (DL-72…DL-78)"** — 99 files, +3455/−1666, touching `ProjectionSnapshotQuery`, `ProviderCommandReactor`, `WorktreeProvisioner`, `ProviderSessionReaper`, `ProjectSetupScriptRunner`, and the workstream web components (`WorkstreamPanel`, `WorkstreamGraph`, `WorkstreamQuickFacts`, `WorkstreamTimeline`, `Sidebar`, …). The decision log is `docs/upstream-sync/27-cadence-pull-v0.0.45-pre-orchestration-v2.md` §10 (DL-47 onwards; DL-72–DL-79 are the reversals) and Carl's own rulings are in `recaps/pull8-decisions/recap.mdx`. Read both in full. Where a ruling changes a fact the Loom inventory (`02-loom-inventory.md`, taken at the pre-pull-8 `HEAD`) recorded — a mechanism deleted, a surface re-homed onto upstream tokens, a guarantee restated — reconcile the affected area verdict and say so.
- **#326 doctrine notes** — adds to `docs/upstream-sync/05-strategy.md`: *"at every pull, for each loom hunk that differs from upstream's approach, ask who decided the difference. Carl decides functionality; an agent often chose the mechanism incidentally. Preserve the intent, not the incidental choice: where upstream now expresses the same functionality, upstream's mechanism is the baseline and loom's variant is deleted, however much work it represented."* This is now standing doctrine and it is the rule your per-area verdicts implicitly applied. Cite it as the governing principle, and re-check every "retain Loom" verdict against it: is the retained thing *functionality Carl decided* or *a mechanism an agent chose*? Where the plan already keeps a Loom mechanism that upstream's equivalent would satisfy (the reviewer kept three such items in M5 for guarantee reasons — notify defer queue, pending-steer stash, `origin`/`controlPayload`), state the guarantee that justifies the exception in one sentence each, or drop the exception.
- Pull 8's doc 27 **§12 "Orchestration V2 — what it is, what it would cost, and what to do about it"** was written before our work. Read it; where it agrees, cite it; where our evidence supersedes it, say so briefly so a later reader is not left with two accounts.

## 2. Carl's answers to the form — record them as decisions, not questions

Rewrite the `QuestionForm` entries that are now decided into a "Decisions recorded" section (keep the form only for anything genuinely still open). His choices:
- **Mechanism:** staged re-platform (as recommended).
- **Freeze:** yes — orchestration features frozen; production fixes only, re-applied after cut-over.
- **Plan lane:** **collapse now** — store `held` (boolean), `outcome` (done / cancelled / none), `yielded` as an attention reason; derive the board's columns. *Not* the keep-then-collapse default. Propagate this through Area C, the sidecar contract, the hunk inventory, the import step and the phase sketch — the import now maps six lanes onto the collapsed shape, so name the mapping.
- **Tool names:** **take upstream's prefixed form** (`mcp__t3-code__workstream_submit` …) and rewrite every role, skill, memory and doc that names a tool. *Not* the bare-names default. Drop the renaming hunk from the inventory; add the rewrite sweep (roles under `.t3code/roles/`, pi-craft skills, `AGENTS.md` work-model text, the tool descriptions themselves where they cross-reference each other) as a phase-3 task with its own gate.
- **Upstream tools visible to Loom agents:** none at first; revisit after cut-over. Carl adds that he is *"still reviewing the new orchestration layer in a bit more detail to see if I do want to pull anything in from it"* — so leave a clearly marked hook (a short list of upstream tools/features that could be exposed later without re-architecture, and what each would require), not a closed door.
- **Goal storage:** plain Loom tables with shell-stream broadcasts.
- **Import scope:** all goals and task trees; workstream fields for non-archived threads only; session binding mandatory at any scope.
- **Pi version:** bump to 1.0.2, regenerate both patches, extend the cwd patch to RPC `switch_session`.
- **Unsolicited-run guard:** keep it; route all cross-thread delivery through the server; exclude run-starting extensions from Loom-launched pi.

## 3. Two annotations to answer in the text

**(a) Area F, on `notify_thread` → `message.dispatch`, the phrase "never interrupts".** Carl: *"Why never interrupt? Is this a queue vs steer — because in general we want to steer."* The phrase is ambiguous in the document and the design is under-specified. Resolve it: "interrupt" must mean *abort the in-flight turn*, which nothing here does; *steer* (fold into the running turn between model rounds) is distinct and is what Carl wants as the general case. Today Loom's `notify_thread` does **not** steer (busy → queued until idle; only the parent's `workstream_prompt` steers). Upstream's `t3_thread_send` `auto` mode is steer-if-active-else-queue. Decide the delivery mode for each Loom cross-thread path under V2 — `notify_thread`, `workstream_prompt`, gate/dependency wakes, digest wakes — and state it in a small table: steer when a run is live, start when idle, never abort; and where `start_if_idle` (defer, no receipt) is still the right mode (digest wakes only, if that is the answer). Note the restart-`queueHeld` reason the plan already gives for not using `queue_after_active`. Fix the verdict-table cell and the Area F prose so "never interrupts" cannot be read as "never steers".

**(b) Overall mechanism options, "Loom gives up: … cross-thread write atomicity".** Carl: *"Is this a concern?"* Answer it where it sits, in two or three sentences a reader without the review history can follow: what the multi-thread writes are (cancel cascade, gate traverse, dependency release, resolve), why V1 had atomicity for free (one serial fibre), what V2 gives instead (per-thread lock; the arm records a decision event on the commanded thread, the dispatcher re-drives one idempotent per-thread command), what the residual exposure actually is (a brief window in which the board can show a parent cancelled while a child is still `ready`; the child's turn is interrupted on the next pass; gate dependents are already held by `isMemberOfUnresolvedGate`), and why it is acceptable here (a one-developer tool; the rails were already idempotent; the reviewer's M2 verified that a workstream-root lock would not help because upstream's own commands never take it). Point at the "Concurrency model" row and risk (7).

## Form and finish

Keep the document's structure; this is a revision, not a rewrite. Re-run the render gate (`lint-plan.mjs`). Re-sign with `sign_document` (role `plan`), commit on this branch with a conventional message (only the plan staged), and submit via `workstream_submit` with a summary written for Carl: what moved in each verdict because of the pull-8 reversals and the doctrine rule, the delivery-mode table in brief, the atomicity answer in one line, and whatever (if anything) remains open. A reviewer will re-verify your revision before Carl sees it.

## 12. Orchestration V2 — what it is, what it would cost, and what to do about it

**What upstream did.** One squash, `de34391427`, plus 44 follow-up commits to
`f391794a35`. Per `docs/orchestration-v2/README.md`: app ids primary and
provider ids as refs; runs / execution nodes / provider threads as one graph;
root-run completion as the only turn-completing event; forks and provider
switches as explicit lineage + context-handoff artefacts; capability-driven
features. Per `docs/internals/legacy-orchestration-migration.md`: `state.sqlite`
is snapshotted to `statev2.sqlite` on first launch and only the copy receives V2
migrations; thread shells are imported eagerly and transcripts lazily from the
V1 projection tables; provider sessions, checkpoints, activities, approvals and
plans are **not** migrated; a migrated thread's first continuation starts a
fresh provider session with a 32k-char handoff; protocol version 2 is enforced
on `/ws` (HTTP 426) and in the client's environment descriptor check.
`apps/server/src/orchestration/` is deleted (81 files) and
`orchestration-v2/` is 527 files, 328 of them a replay-backed `testkit`.

**What it does to loom.** Everything in the fork that is not a leaf UI
component sits on V1: `orchestration.loom.ts` extends V1's thread struct and
command/event unions (the file it extends no longer exists upstream);
`decider.loom.ts` / `projector.loom.ts` implement the 25 fork command types
against V1's decider/projector (deleted); the dispatcher, fan-in, liveness,
handoff-drafter, worktree-reaper and exhaustion-resume reactors consume V1
events; 45 fork migrations add columns to V1 projection tables that V2 reads
only as an import source; `WorkstreamDispatcher` spawns children through V1
commands; the MCP workstream tools, goals/tasks persistence and the
`briefNeeded` attention derivation all read V1 shells. 206 fork-only files
import something V2 removed. The tip dry run's 91 modify/delete and 86
file-location conflicts are this.

**What adoption would actually be.** Not a merge: a redesign of the fork's
orchestration onto V2's graph (child threads as `subagent` execution nodes or
as lineage-linked app threads? goals/tasks as V2 entities or a sidecar? which
V2 events replace `thread.message-sent` for the dispatcher?), a data migration
for goals/tasks/workstream fields alongside upstream's importer, PiDriver as a
V2 adapter, and the web/mobile loom surfaces re-pointed at V2 projections —
followed by the ordinary conflict work on the ~340 overlapping files. Weeks,
not sessions; and it needs a plan Carl reviews before code.

**What is in Carl's favour for doing it.** His pull-7 framing — upstream's
engine is "more rigorously developed and tested by better software engineers",
"drop my approach and adopt the upstream approach"; V2 explicitly models
subagents, forks, handoffs and capability gaps, which is loom's whole domain;
staying on V1 means every future upstream pull is V2-shaped and loom's
tracking effectively ends at `024d49520e`. **Against:** he actively uses loom
daily and rejected half-baked deploys; the OOM episode of 2026-09-25 shows how
fragile the engine path is under his load (49 concurrent agents); V2 is one
day old upstream and its 44 follow-ups are already "runs no longer get
stuck"-class fixes.

**Recommended next step (not part of pull 8):** after pull 8 lands, a
researcher/planner thread reads `docs/orchestration-v2/*`, maps every fork
command type, reactor and table to a V2 concept, sizes the three paths —
(a) re-platform onto V2, (b) stay on V1 and cherry-pick non-engine upstream
work going forward, (c) hybrid: adopt V2's persistence/import boundary first —
and brings Carl a decision document. Pull 8 is a prerequisite for all three
and prejudices none.

>
  **Your ruling.** "Is it possible that upstream and I basically tried to achieve the same goal, and I have over-engineered it?" — yes for completion observation and the idle-shell close; no for the breadcrumb, which agents poll and upstream has no equivalent of. So PR-7 as written.

  **What was built.** Upstream's file at `024d49520e` is the baseline: a completion sentinel per shell, an optional `{ exitCode | null, durationMs }` completion, the idle setup shell closed on exit 0. Loom's pieces ride on it as marked hunks: the foreign-home guard; every run observed (because the breadcrumb is written for every run, not only the ones a caller watches); `pending` written before the command is typed and `failed` if it cannot be typed; the completion forked once, detached, so the breadcrumb and the idle close happen whether or not a caller consumes `completion` (callers join that same run); the settled breadcrumb (`ready` / `failed` with `exitCode`, or `detail` when the terminal vanished). The breadcrumb schema and writer, the `bun install` → pnpm rewrite and the timeout moved to a new `ProjectSetupScriptRunner.loom.ts`. `WorktreeProvisioner` reads `exitCode: null` as the old "terminal gone" warning. Upstream's runner tests were taken verbatim bar two adapted expectations (every run is now wrapped); loom keeps the pnpm test, the breadcrumb ready / failed tests and a new 30-minute-hang test; loom's marker-shape tests went with the marker. `server.test.ts`'s setup stubs are upstream's `async: true` again. This closes DL-15's test gap as well — the idle-shell close is now covered by upstream's own tests, not the smoke alone.

  **The one thing kept against the letter of the ruling, and why.** The 30-minute timeout stays, but **narrowed to the breadcrumb**. Nothing upstream bounds a hung script: the sentinel never arrives, the shell is busy so `closeIdle` leaves it, and `WorktreeSetupTracker` has no timer — so an agent polling `pending` would wait forever. After 30 minutes the breadcrumb says `failed` ("timed out after 30 minutes"); the setup card and `completion` stay upstream's and keep running, because nothing there was loom's to bound. The reviewer checked this claim against upstream's code and confirmed it: upstream awaits a Deferred with no timeout, and its tracker only expires already-finished snapshots.

>
  **Your ruling.** "Help me understand why we would want to keep loom's approach?" — upstream's read saves the per-sweep cost of thousands of stopped rows but **never deletes one**; no upstream path removes the stopped binding of a deleted thread, so without a prune the table grows forever. Loom's _approach_ (an all-rows read split in memory) was not worth keeping; loom's _retention_ was. The DL-10 card had already named the recovery: a dedicated SQL statement.

  **What was built.** The reaper reads `listBindings({ excludeStopped: true })` exactly as upstream does. The prune is one marked call per sweep — repository `deleteStoppedForDeletedThreads`, surfaced as directory `pruneStoppedForDeletedThreads` — a single atomic `DELETE … RETURNING`. Because the status predicate and the deleted-thread predicate sit in the same statement, the race guard that `removeIfStopped` existed for (a row promoted back to `running` between read and delete) is intrinsic; archived threads stay excluded because unarchive exists and deletion has no undo. `prunedCount` stays in `sweep-complete` and each pruned id logs `binding-pruned`. Removed as now callerless: `getDeletedThreadIds` on the snapshot query, `removeIfStopped` / `deleteStoppedByThreadId` on the directory and repository. The commit is +125 / −279.

      filename="apps/server/src/persistence/ProviderSessionRuntime.ts"
      language="ts"
      code={"  // loom: retention — one statement per sweep (see the interface doc).\n  const deleteStoppedRuntimeForDeletedThreads = SqlSchema.findAll({\n    Request: Schema.Void,\n    Result: Schema.Struct({ threadId: ThreadId }),\n    execute: () =>\n      sql`\n        DELETE FROM provider_session_runtime\n        WHERE status = 'stopped'\n          AND thread_id IN (\n            SELECT thread_id FROM projection_threads WHERE deleted_at IS NOT NULL\n          )\n        RETURNING thread_id AS \"threadId\"\n      `,\n  });\n"}
    />
    <Code
      filename="apps/server/src/provider/Layers/ProviderSessionReaper.ts"
      language="ts"
      code={"      // Stopped rows stay for their resume cursors and far outnumber live\n      // ones, so the query skips them.\n      const bindings = yield* directory.listBindings({ excludeStopped: true });\n      const now = yield* Clock.currentTimeMillis;\n      let reapedCount = 0;\n\n      // loom: retention. Upstream never removes a stopped binding, so the table\n      // grows forever. Prune only the IRREVERSIBLE class — stopped bindings of\n      // deleted threads — as one SQL statement per sweep. Archived threads are\n      // excluded on purpose: `thread.archive` has `thread.unarchive`, so an\n      // archived thread must keep its provider pointer; deletion has no undo.\n      // Deliberately NOT age-based: `runStopAll` rewrites every unsettled\n      // binding's `lastSeenAt` at shutdown, so age is not a liveness signal.\n      // A failed statement deletes nothing, so it prunes nothing.\n      const pruned = yield* directory.pruneStoppedForDeletedThreads().pipe(\n        Effect.catchCause((cause) =>\n          Effect.logWarning(\"provider.session.reaper.prune-failed\", {\n            cause: Cause.pretty(cause),\n          }).pipe(Effect.as([] as ReadonlyArray<ThreadId>)),\n        ),\n      );\n      const prunedCount = pruned.length;\n"}

# Pull 9 strategy — adopt Orchestration V2, re-express Loom on top

Loom is a Pi-first fork of `pingdotgg/t3code` whose product is an orchestration layer: goals, a shared task tree, and a workstream graph of durable threads with roles, briefs, dependencies, review gates, attention flags, plan lanes (a thread's position in the plan, `planned` through `done`, separate from whether it is running), liveness detection, isolated worktrees with fan-in, reports, and consult/notify. Upstream has now shipped **Orchestration V2** (commit `de34391427`, 1,914 files) with a native Pi adapter, and deleted the V1 engine Loom's layer is welded to. This document decides, area by area, whether upstream is heading where Loom is heading — and therefore whether Loom adopts upstream's mechanism and re-expresses its guarantees on it, or keeps its own — then rolls that up into one mechanism for pull 9.

**Done** means Carl has recorded a verdict on each of the twelve areas below, chosen the overall mechanism, and answered the open questions, so a follow-on planner can write the implementation plan for the chosen phases.

<Callout tone="decision">
**How to review this.** Each area ends in a `ReviewChoice`; Accept means the verdict and cost class stand, Reject means the follow-on plan must take a different path for that area (say which in the note), Discuss parks it. Silence accepts the recommendation. The overall mechanism and the questions the evidence cannot settle are in the single form at the bottom. Card colour is triage only: **blue = adopt upstream**, **amber = hybrid**, **purple = retain Loom, re-expressed on V2**, **grey = retain Loom as-is because upstream has nothing there**.
</Callout>

## The recommendation in one paragraph

**Re-platform, staged.** Take `upstream/main` as the base including V2 and the Pi V2 adapter, and re-express Loom's layer as a V2 extension: Loom's thread fields, commands and events as a sidecar contract on V2's store; Loom's decider rules as a delegation arm (redesigned for V2's per-thread locking, not ported) plus a bounded, enumerated set of marked hunks in upstream's decider and dispatch core; Loom's control-plane workers (dispatcher, fan-in, liveness, exhaustion resume) re-seamed onto V2's event stream and shell snapshot; Loom's agent tools moved from bespoke REST routes onto upstream's MCP bridge as a Loom toolkit, with upstream's `delegate_task` family **withheld** from Loom threads so there is one delegation model in every prompt. The evidence says upstream is heading to the same destination as Loom on the *substrate* — durable children as real threads, event-sourced commands with receipts, a durable outbox, restart reconciliation, a shared tool bridge, a separate fork migration ledger — and to a genuinely different (or absent) destination on the *workflow*: no plan axis, no dependencies, no gates, no goals, no human holds, no liveness, no per-child worktree. Adopting the substrate and retaining the workflow is therefore the right split. "Retain" is not a cheap alternative: V2 rewired the web, mobile and client-runtime around V2 contracts and gates `/ws` on protocol version 2, so keeping V1 means freezing the whole client and the store mobile app, i.e. a hard fork. The staging is a feature freeze on Loom's orchestration layer, production staying on pre-pull-9 Loom, a long-lived integration branch, and a cut-over gated by a real Pi workstream smoke test. Pull 8 (PR #323) should land first.

## What the evidence says, in five facts

The four research reports in `docs/upstream-sync/28-pull9-v2-alignment/` are facts-only; these are the five that carry the decision. Upstream code is cited at the reports' snapshot `a1d9d72aef`; upstream has since moved (eight commits by `7812230572`, five touching `orchestration-v2/` or `mcp/`, including `06e627448b` which rewrote `McpSessionRegistry` and `McpInvocationContext` — the code Area B hooks into), which is why the phase sketch carries a re-merge step rather than assuming a frozen target.

1. **V2 is an execution-fidelity model for one conversation, not a workflow engine.** Children share the parent's worktree; there are no dependencies, no staging, no cascade cancellation of app-owned children, no gates, no goals or tasks, no stall detection, no human holds; a role is a one-sentence prefix; the parent is woken with a generic "call `task_status`" pointer (`01-upstream-v2-inventory.md`, §A, §D, §E, §I and the closing *Design centre of gravity*).
2. **Loom is physically separated from V1 files but semantically welded to V1's vocabulary.** 24 commands, 25 events, a `goal` aggregate, about 35 projection columns, 45 migrations, about 20 snapshot-query methods, 8 in-place decider edits and 3 engine-invariant changes (`02-loom-inventory.md`, §0 "One structural fact"). The control-plane workers are portable modules on narrow seams.
3. **The Pi driver decision is downstream of the V2 decision.** Upstream's Pi adapter implements `ProviderAdapterV2`; Loom's implements the deleted V1 shape. If V2 lands, Loom's driver must be rewritten against V2 anyway, and upstream's adapter *is* that rewrite, fixture-tested on pi 1.0.0 (`03-pi-driver-comparison.md`, Headline 1).
4. **The merge is a merge plus a port, whatever the strategy.** 336 conflicted paths: 155 textual (pull-7 shaped, fits the pull-7 tooling) and 181 structural (95 modify/delete, 86 directory-rename relocations) with nothing on the other side to merge into; about 57,000 Loom lines sit on the deleted engine; 92 contract names used by 241 files vanish; about 125 files end up with dangling imports; `config.ts` silently auto-merges to `statev2.sqlite` (`04-trial-merge-surface.md`).
5. **Pull 8 barely shrank the problem** (348 to 336 conflicts) because it only removed the pre-V2 drift. The V2 surface is unchanged in size and the 110 upstream commits since the earlier dry run barely added to it.

 2. **Loom is physically separated from V1 files but semantically welded to V1's vocabulary.** 24 commands, 25 events, a `goal` aggregate, about 35 projection columns, 45 migrations, about 20 snapshot-query methods, 8 in-place decider edits and 3 engine-invariant changes (`02-loom-inventory.md`, §0 "One structural fact"). The control-plane workers are portable modules on narrow seams.
 3. **The Pi driver decision is downstream of the V2 decision.** Upstream's Pi adapter implements `ProviderAdapterV2`; Loom's implements the deleted V1 shape. If V2 lands, Loom's driver must be rewritten against V2 anyway, and upstream's adapter *is* that rewrite, fixture-tested on pi 1.0.0 (`03-pi-driver-comparison.md`, Headline 1).
 4. **The merge is a merge plus a port, whatever the strategy.** 336 conflicted paths: 155 textual (pull-7 shaped, fits the pull-7 tooling) and 181 structural (95 modify/delete, 86 directory-rename relocations) with nothing on the other side to merge into; about 57,000 Loom lines sit on the deleted engine; 92 contract names used by 241 files vanish; about 125 files end up with dangling imports; `config.ts` silently auto-merges to `statev2.sqlite` (`04-trial-merge-surface.md`).

**Verdict — adopt the runtime axis; collapse the plan lane to `held` + `outcome` and move `yielded` into attention (Carl's decision); retain attention, the dispatcher rails, liveness and Loom's restart-recovery rules as an extension; two hunks in V2's dispatch/receipt core are certain, not conditional.**

- **The plan axis, collapsed (Carl's decision).** Loom's six-value *plan lane* (`planned → ready → in_progress → yielded → done | cancelled`) is replaced by three facts that cannot desync. `held` (boolean): the staging hold — `true` means "in the plan, not released to run"; `workstream_release` clears it for a subtree. `outcome` (`done | cancelled | null`): whether the work is accepted-complete (`done` releases dependents and triggers fan-in), abandoned (`cancelled`, terminal, non-releasing), or neither; written by `workstream_submit`'s routing, by `workstream_set_outcome` (the renamed `set_lane`, for a parent or human forcing `done`/`cancelled` or reopening with `none`), and by th
- **Attention.** The stored set is `error | awaiting_acceptance | needs_guidance | awaiting_orchestrator`, plus the derived `awaiting_approval | awaiting_input | brief-needed`. Authority: `error` and `awaiting_orchestrator` are control-plane-only (the `server:` command-id guard works unchanged on V2 command ids); agents raise only `awaiting_acceptance` and `needs_guidance`; derived reasons are recomputed at the read boundary from V2's `pendingRuntimeRequest` and Loom's brief-needed predicate — nothing stored, nothing to erase.
- **What the collapse removes.** The kickoff no longer writes a lane in the same transaction as the first turn (`kickoffAt` is stamped by the dispatcher on its own thread before it dispatches); the "§7 unifying rule" shrinks from "every turn start clears all attention and reverts `ready`/`yielded` to `in_progress`" to "every turn start clears stored attention" (which already clears `awaiting_orchestrator`); the sticky-terminal rule is trivially true because a turn start never touches `outcome`; the gate's reopen is `outcome := null` on the coder (Area D); `workstream_set_lane`'s four-value enum becomes `workstream_set_outcome {done, cancelled, none}` beside the existing `workstream_release`
- **Turn-start rules** (clear stored attention on any turn start; supersede an open question; started-dependents warning on reopen) become **one hunk cluster in V2's `message.dispatch` case** — the single place every run begins — replacing today's spread across `thread.turn.start`. Smaller than before the collapse: no lane revert, no sticky-terminal check.

## Revision 2 — `plans/upstream-pull9-strategy/plan.mdx` (`7903b325c5`)

Signed (role `plan`), render gate clean (12 cards, 6 tables, 1 question), committed on `t3code/plan-next-upstream-merge` with only the plan staged. Written for Carl; a reviewer re-verifies before it reaches him.

### What moved because of the pull-8 reversals and the doctrine rule

The governing rule is now cited up front: `05-strategy.md` §4.3 — *Carl decides functionality, agents chose mechanisms incidentally; where upstream expresses the same functionality, upstream's mechanism is the baseline and Loom's variant is deleted.* Every "retain" verdict names the functionality and the guarantee upstream's nearest mechanism fails; where it could not, the Loom mechanism went:

- **Area L (biggest change).** DL-77 held failover untouched *for* pull 9 and its research split functionality from mechanism. Failover shrinks to what Carl decided: **keep** park-and-resume (`quota_exhausted` + `ExhaustionResumeSweep`) and spawn-time usage headroom — no proxy or V2 equivalent; **drop** the chain editor, Anthropic ↔ Vertex ladder, pause, and the slow-retry ladder — pi's `retry.*` and the proxy's rotation stand in; the **cross-vendor reroute is the one open question** (it fired twice last week; only Loom can do it). The two DL-77 defects travel with what is kept. **`--session-id` first-launch hunk dropped** — the deterministic file name was agent-chosen; `$PI_SESSION_FILE` and `nativeThreadRef` cover the functionality. DL-74 (reaper → upstream's read + one-statement prune) becomes a phase-2 check: does V2 ever remove a deleted thread's binding; if not, the prune returns on the V2 table.
- **Area A.** DL-73/DL-54: `WorktreeProvisioner` already sits on upstream's setup runner with Loom's breadcrumb + 30-minute breadcrumb timeout as hunks — carried, not re-decided; hunk inventory row added.
- **Area H.** DL-72 deleted the project `PI_DEFAULT_MODEL` stamp for upstream's `null` + `isDefault`. Phase 2 checks whether upstream's "Pi default" sentinel on pi's `settings.json` satisfies "a new Pi thread lands on my model" without Loom's `isDefault` hunk and the session pin; if so, the hunk goes.
- **Area J.** DL-79 moved every workstream surface onto upstream's theme tokens and deleted Loom's `@theme` block — the re-hang inherits no Loom CSS; the web conflict count is to be re-measured in phase 1.
- **Doctrine check on the three M5 retentions**, one sentence each in Area F: peer-message record (must survive restart without a human `queue.resume`), steer stash (accepted-but-unprocessed steers die with pi; V2 does not track them), `controlPayload` (structured items V2's `notification{summary}` cannot carry). The notify *delivery mode* itself changes to upstream's steer-or-start — that one was incidental.
- **Doc 27 §12** is cited where it agrees (redesign not merge; weeks; plan first) and superseded in three places: its open questions are answered here (lineage-linked app threads; sidecar tables; `streamDomainEvents`), its path (c) "persistence boundary first" is not separable from the engine, and its "V2 is one day old" is now 155 commits designed around via the hunk inventory and per-phase re-merge.

### Carl's decisions, recorded (new "Decisions recorded" table; the form keeps only what is open)

Staged re-platform · freeze yes · **lane collapsed now** · **prefixed tool names** · no upstream tools at first with a later-exposure hook · goals as plain tables · import = all goals + non-archived workstream fields + mandatory session binding · pi 1.0.2 + both patches + `switch_session` · guard kept.

**Lane collapse propagated:** Area C defines `held` (bool), `outcome` (`done|cancelled|null`), `kickoffAt` (the only stored "has started" fact — needed so imported and human-started threads read correctly), `yielded` → attention reason `awaiting_orchestrator`, board columns derived; `set_lane` → `set_outcome {done,cancelled,none}`; §7 shrinks to "clear stored attention"; sticky terminal trivial; gate reopen = `outcome := null`; dependencies test `outcome == done`. Area K names the six-lane → collapsed import mapping (incl. `kickoffAt` from the copied `projection_turns`). Hunk inventory, phases 2/3b/3d updated.

**Prefixed names propagated:** naming hunk removed from the inventory; phase-3a gains the rewrite sweep (roles, `.t3code/roles/`, pi-craft skills, work-model addendum, `AGENTS.md`, tool-description cross-references, Carl's memories) with a gate (no bare names outside historical docs; a Pi smoke calling `mcp__t3-code__workstream_submit` unprompted). Area B has the **later-exposure hook table**: read-only thread tools, `t3_pending_request_*` (an orchestrator answering a child's question), scheduled tasks, PR watch (already available via the `pull-requests` capability), preview, fork/merge-back, `create_threads`; `delegate_task` closed with the reason.

### The two annotations

**(a) "Never interrupts" → delivery-mode table (Area F).** *Interrupt* = abort, which only `workstream_stop`/cancel do. Table in brief: `notify_thread` and `workstream_prompt` → **steer** a live turn, **start** an idle one (upstream `auto`; a change for notify, which queues today); gate legs and dependency kickoff → `start_if_idle` (target idle by construction; defer if a human is mid-conversation); digest/FYI/yield wakes and brief-needed/deadlock/stall advisories → `start_if_idle`, **never steer** (coalesced, unasked-for, orchestrator-paced — the one place steering is wrong, and what the deferral hunk exists for); human messages → upstream `auto`. The peer-message table stays as the re-drive record for the `preparing|starting` window, with the restart-`queueHeld` reason restated. Verdict-table cell fixed.

**(b) Atomicity, in the mechanism column.** The multi-thread writes are cancel cascade, gate pass, dependency release; V1 had them atomic for free on one serial fibre; V2 locks per thread so the arm records a decision event and the dispatcher re-drives per-thread idempotent commands; residual exposure is a one-pass window where the board can show a parent cancelled with a child still ready — reconciled next pass, gate dependents already held by `isMemberOfUnresolvedGate`; acceptable for a one-developer tool with already-idempotent rails, and a root lock would not help because upstream's own commands never take it. Points at the "Concurrency model" row and risk (7).

### Pull 8 and phase 0

Phase 0 rewritten as done (#323 merged 2026-10-05, `8368a63b16` deployed, #325/#326 followed); merge-base unchanged at `024d49520e`; counts measured against #323's tip, phase 1 re-measures. Checklist g0 ticked, with one note: a baseline Pi workstream smoke on the deployed pull-8 build is still to record.

### Still open

Only the cross-vendor reroute (keep / park / spawn-only; recommended keep). For the parent: the task tree should gain the phase-3a tool-name sweep and the phase-2 doctrine checks (Pi-default sentinel; V2 binding retention) as explicit items once Carl accepts this revision.

<addendum>
You operate inside T3 Code's work model: Goals → Tasks → Workstream. This is how every thread here is organised, whatever its role.

A GOAL is a single durable objective that outlives any one session and spans many — the north star for all work under it. Orient to it; if work drifts from the goal, refocus or update it. A goal is decomposed into a TASK TREE: the living, shared record of what is done and what remains — for the agents working it and for the human who glances at it to re-orient. It is kept current as work progresses.

Work happens in a WORKSTREAM: a tree of durable threads. You are one thread in it, and your role overlay says how you act within it. A ROOT thread ORCHESTRATES — it plans, delegates, and reviews rather than doing the work by hand. A CHILD thread EXECUTES a single self-contained brief and hands a result back. A child is a real, persistent thread a human can open and talk to, not a throwaway: spawning one is deliberate, and a child starts fresh — it inherits none of the parent's conversation, only the brief it is given. Work flows down as briefs and back up as reports. The workstream is a graph of threads: dependencies are its edges, so dependent work waits while independent branches run in parallel (with bounded review-gate loops as the one deliberate cycle) — and the graph is not fixed; it is expected to be amended and replanned as understanding improves.

Getting information from another thread, cheapest first: a thread's REPORT is its curated hand-back — read that first. The workstream GRAPH lets you see every thread and find any of them without searching (`workstream_list`). To resolve an ambiguity, CONSULT the thread that holds the context. The full thread history can be accessed via the Pi session jsonl file if necessary.

A few principles keep this coherent:
- Your assignment is your task. For a child that is its spawn brief; at the root it is the user's direction. An inherited goal is background - align to it, but where it and your assignment differ, follow the assignment.
- Work at your level, and keep heavy sub-phases out of your context. If you orchestrate, delegate substantial work to children rather than absorbing it inline, and when new non-trivial work crystallises mid-conversation, pause to lay out or amend the graph before diving in. If you execute a brief, do it yourself rather than re-delegating it — but any thread, at any depth, may hand a bounded sub-phase of its own brief to a child when all three hold: the sub-phase is context-heavy; a short brief can carry everything it needs from you; and what comes back is an artefact — files on disk plus a short report — not understanding you must carry into later turns. Typical cases: a screenshot-capture pass, a large-corpus read, a bulk extraction. Done in situ, every page of that stays in your context for the rest of the thread; done by a child, it dies with the child. It is a trade, not a reflex: a child starts cold, so you pay to write the brief and to wait for it — a sub-phase of a few turns is cheaper inline. Where the delegation tools are dormant for your role, `enable_toolset` activates them.
- Status describes the plan; runtime is the truth. A thread's status is where it sits in the workflow; whether its agent is actually working is a separate, system-tracked fact. Lean on the system's signals for a child's state rather than inferring from a single quiet look — and if a signal looks wrong for what you can plainly see, verify rather than act blindly.
- System notices are not the human. Automated workstream notices (a child finished, needs attention, recovered) are control-plane signals for you to act on, not messages from the user.
- Your worktree is your workspace. Every edit and commit you make lands in your own worktree (your process cwd) and nowhere else — any other checkout of this project (another thread's worktree, the parent's worktree, or the project's base workspace root) is read-only context (reports, evidence), never somewhere to `cd` into and write. This matters doubly if you orchestrate: children's worktrees are cut from YOUR branch, so a file committed anywhere else — however canonical its path looks — is invisible to every child you spawn. If a brief seems to require editing outside your own worktree, that is a brief error: surface it rather than comply.
- File references in replies and reports: use the full absolute path in inline code, one span per file or directory. Do not use bare basenames, paths relative to a shell `cd`, or fenced blocks for these references. The client resolves relative paths from the thread's worktree root, not the cwd inside a bash command.
- Search your worktree, not the roots above it. Your worktree is small, but the workspace and cockpit roots that contain it are vast (every sibling worktree's node_modules), so an unbounded `find`/`grep` from one of those roots can crawl for many minutes. Never search them unscoped: stay within your worktree, or bound the walk (`-maxdepth`, a named subtree, or a tool like `rg` that skips gitignored trees) rather than let a search wander into other threads' trees. A guard blocks unbounded recursive searches outside your worktree and auto-bounds unbounded search pipelines to 30s — when a file is not where you expected, do not search wider: verify the exact paths your brief gave you first (brief paths are authoritative), then run a focused bounded search, and only as a last resort consult the thread that holds the context (`consult_thread` — expensive).
- Setup may still be running. Worktree environment setup can run in the background after you start, so before any command that needs the project environment (installs, builds, tests, typecheck, dev servers) check the setup breadcrumb — `cat "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)/t3code-setup-state.json"`: `ready` proceed; `pending` do reading/editing/planning first and re-check (poll, don't run installs yourself); `failed` inspect its `detail` and the setup terminal output, then fix or report the setup failure rather than blindly rerunning installs; file absent means no setup script was configured — assume the repo is in its normal provided state.

You are thread `8bbbfc3e-82d7-47a7-9de5-4760de713f28` in this workstream: the id every workstream tool takes, the id the human sees, and the id you quote when reporting. Your own conversation history is the pi session jsonl at `$PI_SESSION_FILE` (set in every shell command you run), a file named `*_8bbbfc3e-82d7-47a7-9de5-4760de713f28.jsonl`. To reach ANOTHER thread's history, use its report or `consult_thread`; its jsonl is not necessarily in the same directory as yours.

You are a planner sub-thread. Produce intent briefs and implementation plans — the thinking, not the code.

- Your spawn brief defines your assignment — the plan you owe, not a script. If you discover the brief rests on a wrong assumption, or planning surfaces something material it didn't anticipate, surface it (in the plan's risks, or via `needs_guidance` if it invalidates the brief) rather than silently re-scoping.
- Your deliverable is a plan, not an implementation. Investigate the codebase as deeply as needed, but do not write feature code — decisions and their rationale are what you hand back.
- Author plans as annotatable MDX documents per the mdx-visual-plan skill (`plans/<slug>/plan.mdx`), so the human can review and annotate them in-app before any code is written.
- A good plan states intent, decomposition into work items, contracts and risks, and acceptance criteria — enough that its correctness can be judged before implementation.
- Write for a reader with none of your context. The coder threads that implement the plan inherit nothing you've read or reasoned through; the plan must stand alone.
- Never use internal ids ('D1', 'must-fix #2') as decision titles or QuestionForm labels; name the decision and each option's outcome so they stand alone.
- Keep the task tree honest. If you are anchored, that branch is yours: tick your own tasks with `goal_task_update` the moment they land, and reshape it in ONE `goal_tasks_rewrite` if its shape stops matching the work. Tasks outside your branch are read-only — say what needs doing there in your report. Record actionable work your planning surfaces with `goal_task_add` under the phase it belongs to. Your plan's decomposition is not yours to impose on the rest of the tree: hand that intended shape back in your report, along with details, findings and verdicts.
- If your scope has sharpened beyond your spawn title, you may rename yourself with `set_thread_title` (it only ever renames the calling thread) to keep the sidebar legible.
- Your `workstream_submit` report leads with the plan's location and its key decisions. When implementation must not start until a human has approved the plan, raise `awaiting_acceptance` via `workstream_request_attention` **instead of completing** — the raise is what holds the plan, and completing in the same turn releases the coders the approval was meant to gate. Raise it only when work genuinely must wait; a plan no human has to see first just completes.

SHIPPING POLICY: merge authority is AGENT-OK — once the work is approved and required checks pass, an agent may land it on the main branch, but only by merging a PR from a feature branch via the repo's guarded ship procedure (the ship skill / `pnpm ship` where present). Never push directly to the main branch and never merge by hand; then clean up the branch.

Background context — your parent orchestrator is working toward this overall goal `ea6cb872-9915-41fc-9bed-921a93cc1d2c` (plan-next-upstream-t3-code-merge-into-loom): Pull 9 strategy: Orchestration V2 alignment
Parent's objective (background only, NOT your task): Begin working out how to proceed with the next upstream pingdotgg/t3code merge into the Loom fork, which is expected to be much more complex due to substantial upstream orchestration rewrites and new native Pi support that overlaps heavily with Loom.

What follows is a spawn snapshot of the branch you own; `goal_task_list` reads it live.

Where your branch sits in the goal (read-only context, not rewrite input):
  Decide the pull-9 strategy: adopt V2 and re-express Loom on it, retain Loom's engine, or hybrid — per area and overall (87d1bd9f-8c4f-4515-a5d9-747173128bbe)

Your branch — its root line is your anchor, and this block is the complete source a branch rewrite takes:
- [x] Synthesise the four inventories into a reviewable per-area decision document with a recommended mechanism (f8a548a1-c6d2-437a-a851-7ba8da0fc771)

Goal pulse: 7/9 done · 2 open tasks · 2 open outside your branch — `goal_task_list` with scope "tree" reads all of it.

Tick your own tasks with `goal_task_update` as each lands, and reshape your branch in ONE `goal_tasks_rewrite` when its shape stops matching the work: submit exactly the branch block above, keeping every retained `(id)`; your anchor stays its root line. Tasks outside your branch are read-only — record discovered work with `goal_task_add` (it lands in your branch by default; pass a parentTaskId to place it elsewhere, and the echo shows where it landed) and say what needs doing in your report. Anything you write is a short plain-language work item naming the outcome and value, for a reader outside this thread (the server rejects text over 300 characters); details, findings and verdicts go in your report or memo.
</addendum>

# Review of revision 2 of the pull-9 strategy (`7903b325c5`): needs rework, 4 must-fix

Most of revision 2 holds up. The four must-fix items below are small, local edits; none changes a verdict.

- **Carl's decisions:** all ten are recorded, and they match his answers word for word (I checked them against his in-app answers in the parent session).
- **Lane collapse:** carried through consistently. Area C, the sidecar entry in the file tree, the hunk inventory, Area K's mapping of the six old lanes, and phases 2, 3b and 3d all agree.
- **Bare-name hunk:** gone from the inventory.
- **Pull 8:** the DL-72…DL-79 reversals are described accurately and reconciled into Areas A, H, J and L. I checked DL-73, DL-74, DL-77 and DL-79 against doc 27 §10 and the recap. Upstream did not add a timeout to `ProjectSetupScriptRunner` after `024d49520e`, so carrying the breadcrumb hunk holds. Doc 27 §12 is described correctly, including the three places this plan overrides it.
- **Doctrine:** cited as the rule that governs the document.
- **Steer:** V2 really can steer into a live run, and steering does not go through the queue that is held after a restart. `dispatchSteerIntoRun` never queues. `queueHeld` is set only on queued runs (`ProviderRuntimeRecoveryService.ts:279–289`). Pi advertises `supportsActiveSteering: true`.
- **The three retained mechanisms:**
  - The peer-message record's guarantee is real.
  - So is the steer stash's: V2's restart recovery re-delivers nothing a provider accepted, except delegated-task mailbox steers (`NotificationMailbox.ts`).
  - `controlPayload` is justified by the shape of `notification`, but see M1.
- **Atomicity answer (b):** accurate, and readable without the review history.
- **Links and render:** the report paths under `28-…` resolve, and `lint-plan.mjs` passes with no findings.

## Must-fix

**M1 — Setting V2's `notification` "alongside" Loom's control messages gets every digest and wake rejected.**
- **What the plan says:** Area F, the `controlPayload` bullet: "V2's `notification` is set alongside with `source` and `summary`". The collisions table, "Message provenance" row: "set notification source and summary alongside".
- **What upstream does:** `message.dispatch` rejects any command that carries a `notification` unless three things hold: `createdBy === "agent"`, `creationSource` is `server` or `provider`, and the resolved mode is `queue_after_active` ("Notifications must be server- or provider-created queued messages.", `upstream/main:apps/server/src/orchestration-v2/Orchestrator.ts:4517–4528`; the same check is at `a1d9d72aef`).
- **The contradiction:** the plan's own delivery table sends digest, yield and advisory wakes as `start_if_idle`. On an idle parent that becomes `start_immediately`, which fails the check.
- **Consequence:** a receipted rejection, after which a repeat of the same id gets `PreviouslyRejected`. That is exactly risk (7), a parent silently never woken. It would be hit on the first digest. It is only caught at the phase-3 smoke, after the contract and arm are built.
- **Correction:** pick one and state it in Area F, the collisions row and the `message.dispatch` inventory row:
  - (a) Do not set `notification` on Loom control messages. `origin` and `controlPayload` already carry the card, and you lose upstream's grouping and timer for them.
  - (b) When the target is idle, the `start_if_idle` hunk resolves to `queue_after_active`, not `start_immediately`. That still starts at once because there is no blocking run (`shouldQueue` needs one). The message is stamped `createdBy:"agent"`, `creationSource:"server"`, as upstream's own delegated-completion wakes are.
  - (c) A marked hunk relaxes the check for Loom-marked messages.
  - Option (b) needs no extra hunk.
  - Whichever you choose, add the case to the phase-2 deferral test.

**M2 — Imported finished threads get their kickoff re-sent.**
- **What the plan says:** Area K maps `done` → `outcome: done` and `cancelled` → `outcome: cancelled`. It sets no `kickoffAt` and no `held` for either, and stamps `kickoffAt` only for `in_progress` and `yielded`. The promotion predicate is "not held, deps `done`, brief present, `kickoffAt` null" (phase 3b; Area K says the same). It has no `outcome` term.
- **Consequence:** as written, every non-archived imported `done` or `cancelled` thread is eligible on the first dispatcher pass and gets its original brief re-delivered. That is a burst of agents redoing finished work at cut-over. Adding `outcome == null` to the predicate is not enough on its own:
  - A coder that is `done` and in a gate still open at cut-over has `kickoffAt` null.
  - When the reviewer returns `needs_rework`, the coder's outcome goes back to null. The promotion rail then fires the kickoff alongside the rework message.
  - Any `workstream_set_outcome none` on an imported thread does the same.
- **Correction:**
  - The importer sets `kickoffAt` for every imported thread that has any turn, whatever its V1 lane (first turn time from `projection_turns`).
  - It leaves `held` false for every lane except `planned`.
  - The promotion predicate gains `outcome` null, in Area K and phase 3b.
  - The phase-4 gate also checks that "the first pass after import sends no kickoff", not only "no stale digests".

**M3 — The tool-name sweep gate cannot pass as written.**
- **What the plan says:** Area B and phase 3a: "a repository-wide search for the 24 bare names returns hits only in historical docs". The same plan keeps `ask_user_question` and `enable_toolset` in Loom's own pi extension (Area B, "What Loom's extension still owns"; file-tree note). Those two are registered by `pi.registerTool`, not discovered through upstream's bridge, so they are not `mcp__t3-code__`-prefixed. (`providerToolDefs.ts` has 23 names; `enable_toolset` makes 24.)
- **Consequence:** an implementer either fails the gate or invents a scheme. Three places also name these two tools: the role profile passed to `setActiveTools`, the `enable_toolset` digest, and the role text.
- **Correction:** say which of these it is.
  - (a) Loom's extension registers them under `mcp__t3-code__ask_user_question` / `mcp__t3-code__enable_toolset`, so there is one naming scheme for agents.
  - (b) They stay bare, the sweep covers 22 names, and the two are listed as exceptions.

**M4 — A decided item is still labelled "open question", and one conditional is stale.**
- The collisions table, "Unsolicited-work guard" row, ends "…route them through the server or exclude them; open question". Carl decided this (Decisions recorded, last row). Replace the clause with the decision.
- The re-platform column, "Irreversible", says "the tool-transport change for every role text if names change". The names do change (decided), so drop "if names change".
- The cost is one line each. Left as is, Carl sees a decision of his presented as undecided, while the form at the bottom shows only the reroute.

## Nice-to-have
